title: European robin
summary: The European robin (Erithacus rubecula): a small songbird, about 14 cm long and 19 g, with an orange face and breast.

layers.basics: This is the robin of British gardens and parks: a plump little bird with an orange-red face and breast, a brown back, a pale belly and thin legs. It stands here, alert, on a boulder. Use the layer buttons to peel it: feathers, skin, muscles, skeleton, organs, air sacs and lungs, nerves. Click any part for its card. The bird is drawn at the size of a typical adult and the organs are drawn by eye, so zoom right in and read each card's note on what is measured and what is drawn.
layers.deeper: A robin is a passerine, a perching bird. Its body is built for flight with very little weight: hollow bones, a big keel on the breastbone to hold the flight muscles, a fused hand, feathers, and a lung that works with air sacs. Its song, its territory and the orange breast that rivals read as a signal are all part of how it lives. The cards link each part to the human structure it matches (a wing is an arm) and to the molecules at the bottom of the scale.
layers.expert: The model is a procedural reconstruction. Overall size and the published feather counts (10 primaries, 9 secondaries including 3 tertials, 12 tail feathers) are used; the proportions of every part and the size and place of every organ are drawn by eye from photographs and anatomical drawings and are approximate. Colours follow the plumage description in the sources. The bird stands still; breathing and the heartbeat are illustrations, not measured movements.

about 2 years once it reaches breeding age; UK ringing record 8 years 4 months (BTO)

title: How a robin flies
summary: A flying bird gets lift from air flowing over its wings; flapping tilts that force forward to push the bird along.

layers.basics: Lift is a force at right angles to the air flowing past a wing. The wing is shaped and tilted so that the air curves around it and ends up pushed downward, and by the same exchange the wing is pushed up. It is not enough to say that flapping pushes air down: the wing makes lift because air is moving over it, which is why a bird gliding with its wings still held out stays up. In flapping flight the downstroke makes the lift and most of the forward push; on the upstroke the wing is folded a little to cut the cost.
layers.deeper: The muscles that move the wing tilt the lift forward, so part of the force is thrust that beats the drag and raises speed, and the higher speed makes more lift to balance weight. A bird changes the angle of its wing to the air all the time during each beat and as its speed changes. The alula, the small group of feathers at the front of the wrist, helps hold the airflow on the wing at low speed, as when landing. Energy lost to lift-induced drag ends up mainly in vortices shed from the wing tips.
layers.expert: The lift on a wing of area S in air of density ρ at speed v is L = ½ρv²S·C_L, where the lift coefficient C_L rises with the angle of attack up to the stall. Wing loading (weight divided by wing area) sets how fast a bird must fly: a high loading goes with short pointed wings and rapid beats, a low loading with long wings and slow flight. The bird in this model stands still: it is not drawn in flight, and the 3-D wings are folded.

facts: makes lift and provides most of the thrust
wing folded slightly inward to reduce the energy cost
feathers of the "thumb" that help avoid stalling at low speed

title: Song, and how a bird sings two notes at once
summary: A robin sings with its syrinx, a voice box at the base of the windpipe. Experiments on other songbirds show it is the soft lips (labia) inside it that vibrate, and that some species can control its two sides separately.

layers.basics: A bird does not sing with its throat the way you do. The sound is made deep in the chest, where the windpipe splits in two to go to the lungs. That organ is the syrinx. As air from the lungs passes through, soft tissue folds in each bronchus vibrate, and muscles change their tension. In some songbirds the two sides can be controlled separately, so one bird can make two sounds at once. The mouth and windpipe above then shape the sound.
layers.deeper: In songbirds the syrinx lies where the windpipe forks (the tracheobronchial form). Goller and Larsen (1997) removed the thin membranes (the medial tympaniform membranes) that textbooks had said make the sound, and zebra finches and northern cardinals still sang nearly normally. Endoscope pictures in a crow, cardinals and brown thrashers showed two soft lips, the medial and lateral labia, moving whenever sound was made, so the labia are the likely source. The pessulus, the bony wedge at the fork, is a support and was not seen to vibrate. Northern mockingbirds, brown thrashers and gray catbirds have been shown to use the two sides independently. Both sexes of robin sing, all year round, and a male starts morning song about an hour before sunrise.
layers.expert: The independent control of the two sides varies between songbirds: canaries and chaffinches rely strongly on the left side, thrashers and catbirds use both sides about equally, and only a small number of species has been sampled. No study found shows it for the European robin. In Goller and Larsen's endoscopy the imaging was too slow to measure the frequency of the labial vibration, so the labia are a strong candidate, not a proven source. The cut-open syrinx in the model is a simplified drawing at the size of an adult; the labia are not drawn.

facts: at the fork of the windpipe, above the lungs
labia (soft lips) in each bronchus most likely; membranes not essential (Goller and Larsen 1997)
shown in mockingbirds, thrashers and catbirds; not shown for the robin
starts about an hour before sunrise (European robin article)
open_questions: Does the European robin control the two sides of its syrinx independently, as mockingbirds and thrashers do? Nobody appears to have shown it.

title: Robins, noise and light: when they sing
summary: In a Sheffield survey, robins sang at night at the places that were noisiest by day; in other studies artificial light made robins start their dawn song earlier.

layers.basics: A robin that sings at night near a street light is a familiar puzzle. Two sets of studies give two parts of the answer. A survey in the English city of Sheffield found that the places where robins sang at night were much noisier by day, and light did not explain the pattern once the noise was counted. Studies in Germany and Finland found that light at night, not traffic noise, made robins and other songbirds start their dawn song earlier.
layers.deeper: The Sheffield study (Fuller, Warren and Gaston 2007) visited 121 locations once by day and once at night. Robins sang by day at 67 and at night at 18 of those; the night-singing places were louder by day (about 63 dB against about 53 dB), and the light effect vanished once daytime noise was included. Da Silva and colleagues (2014) compared woodland plots with light, noise, both or neither and found that artificial light, but not noise, led to earlier dawn singing in five of six species. In the 2015 study of six species at lit and unlit sites in Germany the robin's dawn song began earlier with light, and a study in Finland found robins starting earlier as the natural night brightness rose.
layers.expert: The studies measured different things: night singing in Sheffield, and the time dawn song starts in the others. So they do not contradict each other, and they leave the cause of true night singing open. In the 2015 model the light effect for the robin on the start of dawn song was positive and clear (coefficient 3.5, standard error 0.8, p below 0.001); the size in minutes is not given there for the robin. A summary of the 2014 paper gives about 10 to 20 minutes earlier, with about 20 minutes for the robin, which was not checked in the full text.

facts: ≈ 63 dB at night-singing sites, ≈ 53 dB at day-only sites (light not significant once noise was counted: p = 0.947, noise p = 0.002)
earlier start in lit sites in five of six species (Da Silva et al. 2014); in the robin too (2015)
open_questions: Is singing at night in towns a response to daytime noise, to artificial light, or both? Light is clearly linked to earlier dawn song, but true night singing is still debated.

title: Territory, and the red breast as a signal
summary: A robin defends a territory, and its red breast seems to be what rivals respond to: in David Lack's experiments a stuffed robin and even a bundle of red feathers could provoke an attack.

layers.basics: Male robins defend a patch of ground fiercely against other males, and sometimes against other small birds and even their own reflection. David Lack put stuffed robins into the territories of living ones. The residents attacked them, and some birds even attacked a bundle of red feathers on its own, which suggests the red breast is the signal that releases the attack.
layers.deeper: Lack's fieldwork was at Dartington Hall; his book The Life of the Robin appeared in 1943. In one account of his experiments, a hen robin attacked the empty space where red feathers had been. Accounts differ in detail and the red-feather result applied to some of the birds tested, not all. Fights are costly: territorial disputes are reported to cause a share of adult deaths in some studies. Both sexes sing and defend ground, and song is a second signal that tells neighbours where the owner is.
layers.expert: The experiments show that red feathers released an aggressive response in those birds, which fits the idea that the breast works as a signal to an intruder. They do not by themselves show why red evolved or what the colour says about the bird.

facts: stuffed robins in territories; a bundle of red feathers could provoke attack in some birds
reported as a cause of some adult deaths; the share is not established here
open_questions: What does the colour and size of the red patch tell a rival, and how did it evolve as a signal?

title: Migration: some robins travel, many stay
summary: British and Irish robins mostly stay put; robins from Scandinavia and Russia move west and south for the winter.

layers.basics: In Britain and Ireland most robins are residents all year. A small minority, mostly females, leave for southern Europe, some as far as Spain. Robins breeding in Scandinavia and Russia are the long-distance ones: they migrate to Britain and western Europe to escape harsher winters, which is why there are more robins in British gardens in winter.
layers.deeper: A population can contain both residents and migrants, so migration is a habit that varies within a species, not a single trait. The robin is also the best-known test animal for the question of how migrating birds keep direction, which leads to the compass card.
layers.expert: The shares of residents and migrants vary between populations and years. Migrants are described as greyer above and duller orange below than residents.

facts: largely resident; a small minority (usually females) goes to southern Europe, some to Spain
migrate to Britain and western Europe for winter

title: Body temperature and heart rate
summary: Birds run hotter than mammals: about 41 °C when active on average, and a small songbird's heart beats several hundred times a minute.

layers.basics: A robin is warm-blooded and runs hotter than you: birds in general average about 38.5 °C at rest and about 41 °C when active. Its heart is small and very fast. For scale, a similar-sized songbird, the tropical spotted antbird of about 17 g, was measured in the wild at between 260 beats a minute at night and 824 a minute by day.
layers.deeper: In a review of body temperatures in birds, the mean was 38.54 ± 0.96 °C in the resting phase (203 birds), 41.02 ± 1.29 °C in the active phase (724) and 43.85 ± 0.94 °C in high activity (74). Passerines run slightly high in the active phase. The animation of the heart in this model is an illustration with no real rate. For scale, hummingbirds have been recorded with heart rates up to 1,200 beats a minute (Lasiewski 1964).
layers.expert: Heart rate and oxygen use rise together, so a heart-rate record can stand in for the energy a bird spends. Many birds lower their body temperature a little at night as a way to save energy. The antbird numbers are for another species in a rain forest, and the temperatures are means over many bird species: neither is a measurement on robins,.

title: How long a robin lives
summary: Many robins die in their first year; one that reaches breeding age typically lives about two years, and ringing records are far longer.

layers.basics: Robins have a short average life because so many die in their first year: the BTO gives first-year survival of about 41 %. A robin that reaches breeding age typically lives about two years. The oldest ringed wild robin in Britain reached 8 years, 4 months and 30 days (ringed bird, 1977), and the longest record in the European ringing records is a Czech bird of 19 years 4 months.
layers.deeper: Records depend on the ringing scheme that holds them: the BTO record is for birds ringed in Britain and Ireland, and the EURING list of European records holds a longer one (a Czech robin found dead at 19 years 4 months, and a Dutch one at 17 years 11 months). A bird ringed as an adult has a minimum age only. Heavy first-year mortality is why the average is far below the maximum.
layers.expert: The adult annual survival given by the BTO is about 0.42 and first-year survival about 0.41. A figure of about 1.1 years for average life expectancy is repeated in popular accounts but was not found in a BTO or RSPB source here, so it is not used. Territorial fights are reported to cause a share of adult male deaths in some studies; the size of that share is not established.

facts: Typical life once breeding age is reached
usually 2 a year, 4 to 5 eggs (2 to 9), incubation 14 to 16 days, fledging at 12.5 to 16 days (BTO)

title: Birds are living dinosaurs
summary: Birds are theropod dinosaurs: the robin is a descendant of feathered dinosaurs that lived over 150 million years ago.

layers.basics: A robin is a dinosaur, in the same way you are a mammal. Birds belong to the theropods, the group that includes Velociraptor and Tyrannosaurus, and many theropods had feathers. Fossils of more than thirty feathered non-bird dinosaurs have been collected, many in Liaoning in China. Features that birds share with some of those dinosaurs include a wishbone, hollow bones and, in a few kinds, a gizzard that held stones.
layers.deeper: The present consensus is that birds are maniraptoran theropods that originated in the Jurassic, roughly 165 to 150 million years ago. Sinosauropteryx (found in 1996) was covered in filaments; they were once interpreted as having a central shaft with branches, and later work prefers simple filaments, so their structure is still discussed. Anchiornis, a small feathered dinosaur with long arm and leg feathers, lived before Archaeopteryx. Archaeopteryx, from the Late Jurassic limestone of Solnhofen in Germany, is about 150 million years old (early Tithonian). Gizzard stones are known from some theropods (the ornithomimosaur Sinornithomimus and the oviraptorosaur Caudipteryx), but swallowed stones can also be accidental, so this is a feature of some theropods, not all.
layers.expert: Debated within the consensus: the exact sequence of changes among the maniraptorans; which digits the bird hand keeps (II-III-IV in the embryo, I-II-III in the fossils); and whether the earliest flapping evolved from the ground up, from the trees down or with wing-assisted running up slopes. Evidence that non-bird theropods had air-sac lungs like those of birds exists for at least one theropod (Majungatholus) and is taken to suggest that one-way airflow was general among theropods.

facts: Jurassic, roughly 165 to 150 million years ago
more than 30 species with preserved feathers
about 150 million years old (150.8 to 148.5 million years; early Tithonian)
wishbone, hollow bones; gizzard stones in some kinds (not all)
open_questions: Which digits of the bird hand are which (II-III-IV from embryos, I-II-III from fossils)?
How did flight begin: from the ground up, from the trees down, or by running up slopes?

title: A magnetic compass sense
summary: Robins sense Earth's magnetic field: that is shown by their behaviour. What the sensor is, is not known; a light-sensitive protein in the eye, cryptochrome, is the leading idea, and a magnetite-based sense has been proposed too.

layers.basics: The European robin is one of the migratory songbirds used to test how birds find direction. Experiments over fifty years show that a robin can use Earth's magnetic field as a compass, and that this compass reads the angle of the field lines (their tilt against gravity) and not which end is north. What the robin uses to detect the field is not known. The leading hypothesis is a protein in the eye called cryptochrome: when light hits it, two electrons are moved and a pair of molecules, each with an unpaired electron, forms. Earth's weak field could change how long that pair lasts.
layers.deeper: What behaviour has shown: robins use the inclination of the field (Wiltschko and Wiltschko 1972); weak oscillating radio-frequency fields disturb their orientation (Ritz et al. 2004) and so does man-made electromagnetic noise, and screening the huts restores it (Engels et al. 2014); and damage to a visual forebrain area (cluster N) removes the magnetic compass, while cutting the trigeminal nerve does not (Zapka et al. 2009). What the cryptochrome experiments measured: Xu and colleagues (2021) made robin cryptochrome 4 in the laboratory and found it more magnetically sensitive than the same protein from the chicken and the pigeon, two non-migratory birds. The test was on purified protein in a tube, at 5 °C, and the effects were seen at about 30 millitesla, hundreds of times stronger than Earth's field of about 50 microtesla.
layers.expert: The authors report that the radical pair in purified robin cryptochrome 4 lasts about 100 nanoseconds, roughly ten times too short (about 1 microsecond) for a response at Earth-strength field, and say the protein would need to be anchored, aligned and linked to signalling partners to respond at Earth strength. The work did not show the effect in a living bird. The competing idea is a sense based on magnetite (iron oxide) in the beak, proposed for pigeons (Mora et al. 2004); the iron-rich cells seen in pigeon beaks were later shown to be macrophages, not nerve cells (Treiber et al. 2012). Robins are thought by some researchers to have two magnetic senses, one light-dependent and one trigeminal.

facts: robins orient by a light-dependent inclination compass (1972 onwards)
more sensitive than chicken and pigeon cryptochrome 4; seen at about 30 mT, not at Earth-strength field
about 100 ns in purified wild-type protein, against about 1 µs needed at Earth strength
the compass is shown by behaviour; the sensor is a hypothesis, not shown in a living bird
open_questions: Is cryptochrome 4 the robin's magnetic sensor in the living eye, or is a magnetite-based sense involved too?
How is a magnetically sensitive chemical signal read out by the nerves, and how does it work in a living cell at Earth-strength field?

title: Keratin: the protein of feathers, bill and claws
summary: Feathers, beak and claws are made mostly of beta-keratin, a tough protein held together by sulfur bridges between cysteine units.

layers.basics: The hard, light stuff of a feather is a protein called keratin. In birds and reptiles it is a special kind, beta-keratin, built of sheets that are twisted together and locked by sulfur-to-sulfur bridges. Those bridges come from the amino acid cysteine. The keratin molecule itself is not in this explorer's molecule data; its building block, cysteine, and the linked pair, cystine, are.
layers.deeper: Beta-keratins are found only in birds and reptiles. In feathers, beaks and claws they are formed mainly as beta-pleated sheets, stabilised by disulfide bridges between cysteine residues. Birds also have alpha-keratins, the family that makes up hair and horn in mammals, for example in parts of the skin. Because a bridge cannot be undone without a chemical reaction, a feather is a long-lived, heat-stable material.
layers.expert: The sauropsid beta-keratins are encoded by a different gene family from alpha-keratins; the name "corneous beta proteins" has been proposed to avoid the confusion. Human hair is about 14 % cysteine for comparison (not measured on feathers).

title: What colours the robin's feathers
summary: Brown feathers get their colour from melanin; the orange of the breast is classed as melanin-based in one study, but its pigment has not been shown by chemical analysis.

layers.basics: Feather colour comes from pigments and from structure. The two common pigment groups are melanins (browns and blacks) and carotenoids (reds, oranges and yellows that a bird gets from its food). The robin's brown back is melanin. For the orange breast, a study that measured the colour of four European songbirds grouped the robin's breast with the melanin-based colours; the authors say this is the main mechanism and that the classification rested on the usual understanding, not on chemical tests.
layers.deeper: The paper (Delhey and colleagues 2010) measured 236 robin samples over three years. It suggests that a red feather may be coloured by phaeomelanin, the reddish form of melanin, which is the dominant pigment in many red plumages. A carotenoid colour cannot be ruled out without extracting the pigment from robin breast feathers. For that reason this explorer does not draw a carotenoid molecule here.
layers.expert: Melanin is made from the amino acid tyrosine through L-DOPA; the molecule data has L-DOPA, tyrosine, and also beta-carotene, which is only an example of the carotenoid group. Birds cannot make carotenoids and take them in food; whether a robin does so for its breast is not shown.

facts: classed melanin-based; pigment not tested by chemistry
open_questions: Which pigment colours the robin's orange breast: phaeomelanin, a carotenoid, or both? It needs chemical analysis of the feathers.

title: How a robin breathes: air that flows one way
summary: A bird's lungs are fed by air sacs, so air flows through the lung in one direction during both breathing in and breathing out.

layers.basics: You breathe in and out through the same tubes, so the air in your lungs goes back and forth. A bird's air passes through its lungs in one direction all the time, because the lungs are connected to air sacs that act as bellows. Fresh air goes first to the sacs at the back, then through the lung, then to the sacs at the front and out.
layers.deeper: The air sacs do not exchange gas; the lung tubes (parabronchi) do. Flow irreversibility at the junctions of the airways keeps the flow in one direction, so the lung gets fresh air during both the breath in and the breath out. A tracer in a duck stayed in the bird for two breath cycles.
layers.expert: Birds typically have nine air sacs; passerines are counted as having seven because two sacs may be fused. The model draws nine. In a tracer-gas study of zebra finches and blackbirds, breathing rates rose from 1.5 to 2.3 breaths per second in calling and to 3.5 in wing-flapping.

title: How a robin keeps hold of a twig
summary: A tendon behind the ankle tightens when the leg bends, curling the toes round a perch with little effort.

layers.basics: A bird can stand on a twig all night without tiring. When it squats, the ankle bends and a long tendon is pulled tight; the tendon pulls the toes shut around the perch. The tendon and the tissue around it are rough, which locks the grip until the leg straightens again. The ankle is the joint that looks like a backward knee. In the standing pose shown here, the toes rest flat on the boulder, so the lock is not engaged.
layers.deeper: A robin's foot has three toes pointing forward (toes II, III and IV) and one back (the hind toe, toe I): the usual arrangement in perching birds and nearly all songbirds. The toe bones number 3, 4 and 5 in the three forward toes and 2 in the hind toe.
layers.expert: A 2012 study of European starlings found that sleeping birds bent their knees only slightly, not enough to engage the lock, and balanced on the central pad of the foot, so the lock may matter less than the popular explanation says.

facts: the joint between the tibiotarsus and tarsometatarsus
open_questions: How much do birds depend on the tendon lock while perching and sleeping?

title: Hollow bones with struts
summary: Many bird bones are hollow and air-filled, braced inside by thin struts: light, but stiff.

layers.basics: A bird's skeleton has to be light enough to fly. Many of its bones are hollow tubes filled with air, with thin struts across the inside like the braces in a bridge. The air comes from the air sacs, which reach into some bones. The whole skeleton is only about 5 % of a bird's weight, and in many birds the feathers probably weigh more than the skeleton. Not every bird has hollow bones: penguins, loons, puffins and kiwis do not.
layers.deeper: Pneumatised bones are shared with the theropod dinosaurs that birds came from. In a tube, strength comes from the wall and from the distance of material from the axis, so a thin hollow wall can match a solid rod of much greater mass.
layers.expert: The statement about feathers comes from a rough estimate (Brodkorb 1955) from feather counts, not from weighing a robin; no figure is given for a robin. The extent of hollow bone differs between species and between bones, and how far it reaches in a small songbird varies bone by bone. The tissue scene is a general picture of a hollow bird bone, not a measurement on a robin.

title: Crown
summary: The top of the head: olive-brown, running back from just above the forehead.

layers.basics: The crown is brown, with an olive tinge in British birds, and sits like a cap above the orange face. Click a part and look at the layer buttons to see what lies under it: skin, then the skull.
layers.deeper: The head feathers are small contour feathers laid like tiles. Like those of the nape and back, they are coloured by melanin. Young robins are spotted brown and white, and the orange appears gradually.
layers.expert: The borders between the brown crown and the orange face and the grey neck are drawn jagged on purpose; in life they are the edges of feather tracts and the feathers overlap.

facts: spotted brown and white; orange appears gradually

title: Nape and neck
summary: The back of the head and the neck: olive-brown, over the long neck bones.

layers.basics: The nape is the back of the neck. It is brown like the crown and back. Under the feathers lies a long, flexible neck made of many small vertebrae, typically 14 in songbirds against seven in a person.
layers.deeper: The feathers sit in rows (tracts) on bare skin between them. The neck lets the robin turn its head far back to preen and to look along its body with each eye.
layers.expert: The neck is covered by contour feathers and downy feathers beneath; the model draws only one smooth outline for the neck feathers.

title: Face and throat
summary: The orange face, chin and throat: the front of the signal patch, edged with grey on the sides of the neck.

layers.basics: The face is orange from the forehead and the eye down to the chin and throat, and runs on into the breast. Males and females look alike. The eye sits in the orange, with a thin pale ring round it.
layers.deeper: In Lack's experiments a bundle of red feathers could provoke territorial attack in some birds, so the orange front of a robin is treated as a likely signal to rivals. How the pigment is made is not proved (see the colour card).
layers.expert: The face is made of small feathers that end in bristle-like tips around the bill base (rictal bristles) in many birds; the model draws only the smooth outline.

facts: orange face and breast, edged with bluish grey

Delhey et al. 2010: Seasonal changes in colour (PLoS ONE; robin, blackbird, blue tit, great tit)

title: Breast
summary: The orange breast: the robin's famous signal, bordered by grey at the sides.

layers.basics: This is the orange-red that gives the robin its name. It sits over the large flight muscles of the breast. Rivals seem to read it as a threat: a bundle of red feathers alone could provoke an attack in some birds in Lack's experiments.
layers.deeper: The breast feathers overlap like roof tiles and are thick enough to hold a layer of air against the skin. Their colour was classed as melanin-based by Delhey et al. 2010, without a chemical test.
layers.expert: Under the feathers and skin the large pectoral muscles cover the keeled breastbone. The shape of the breast changes as the bird fluffs its feathers.

facts: a bundle of red feathers could provoke attack (Lack)

ext.title: Delhey et al. 2010: Seasonal changes in colour (PLoS ONE; robin, blackbird, blue tit, great tit)
