title: Grey border of the breast
summary: A band of bluish grey between the orange breast and the brown back, on the sides of the neck and chest.

layers.basics: The orange face and breast are edged on the sides of the neck and chest with bluish grey. The grey makes the orange stand out.
layers.deeper: Grey in feathers is usually a dilute black melanin. Blue-looking colours in feathers can also come from fine structure that scatters light, so the origin of the blue tinge is a separate question.
layers.expert: The colour in the model is a flat grey; the real band is feathered and graded.

title: Back (mantle and scapulars)
summary: The olive-brown upper back and the long shoulder feathers that cover the folded wing's root.

layers.basics: The back is olive-brown, a colour that probably helps hide the robin on the ground or in a hedge. Its folded wings lie over the sides of it.
layers.deeper: The scapular feathers are long feathers growing along the shoulder blade; they lie over the base of the folded wing.
layers.expert: The brown is melanin-based in the Delhey et al. 2010 classification.

ext.title: Delhey et al. 2010: Seasonal changes in colour (PLoS ONE; robin, blackbird, blue tit, great tit)

title: Rump
summary: The lower back above the tail, where the tail feathers are anchored.

layers.basics: The rump is the rear of the back, just in front of the tail. Under its feathers the fused hip bones and the stub of the tail bones lie.
layers.deeper: The upper tail coverts spring from here and cover the roots of the tail feathers. The preen gland (uropygial gland) of many birds lies on the rump; it is not drawn in this model.
layers.expert: The rump plumage is slightly warmer brown in the model.

facts: plumage over the pelvis, the base of the tail

title: Flank
summary: The side of the body between the wing and the belly: buff-brown.

layers.basics: The flank is the side of the belly, below the folded wing and above the leg. The thigh is hidden under these feathers; only the lower leg shows.
layers.deeper: The leg has a "knee" hidden in the flank plumage: what looks like a backward knee below it is the ankle.
layers.expert: Flank feathers are loose and fluff out; they help insulate the thigh.

title: Belly
summary: The pale belly: whitish, in contrast with the orange breast above it.

layers.basics: The belly is whitish. It covers the soft organs: the gizzard, liver and intestines, with the air sacs round them.
layers.deeper: The belly feathers are denser at the sides; a bird in cold weather fluffs them to trap air.
layers.expert: Under the belly lies the posterior part of the body cavity; the keel of the breastbone does not reach the rear.

title: Vent and undertail area
summary: The feathers round the single opening for gut, kidneys and reproduction, the cloaca.

layers.basics: The vent is the area around the cloaca: birds use one opening for droppings, urine and reproduction. The feathers of the undertail cover the base of the tail from below.
layers.deeper: The kidneys excrete nitrogen as uric acid, which is semi-solid; it leaves with the faeces.
layers.expert: The cloaca is also the opening of the reproductive tract; the same opening serves the reproductive tract.

title: Bill: upper and lower mandible
summary: The bill is a thin, pointed horny sheath over the jaw bones: the robin's tweezers for picking up small food.

layers.basics: The bill has two halves, the upper and lower mandible. They are covered with a hard, horny sheath of keratin and are black in a robin. A robin uses its bill like tweezers to pick up small food. Birds have no teeth: the bill and the gizzard do the work.
layers.deeper: The horn sheath (the rhamphotheca) is made of keratin, which is dead material, but it grows continuously from living tissue at the base of each half of the bill and wears away at the tip. Inside, the upper jaw is a slender bone core (the premaxilla), and the lower jaw hinges at the quadrate bone. The nostrils open on the top of the upper mandible near its base.
layers.expert: The sheath is beta-keratin, like feathers and claws. All living birds can move the upper jaw relative to the braincase (cranial kinesis), most obviously in parrots; how far a robin's bill flexes is not measured here.

title: Nostrils
summary: The two small openings in the upper bill near its base, through which air reaches the nose.

layers.basics: Birds breathe in through two small openings, the nares, near the base of the upper bill. They lead into the nasal passages, then down the windpipe.
layers.deeper: Air entering through the nostrils is warmed, moistened and filtered in the nasal passages and the upper windpipe before it reaches the lungs. Many birds have a feather-covered flap over the opening; a robin has none that matters here.
layers.expert: The nostrils open on the upper bill, not at its tip as in a mammal, which is a description, not an explanation: the reason for the position is not stated. The model draws two small ovals.

title: Eye
summary: A robin's eye is dark and large for the size of its head.

layers.basics: The black bead you see is the front of the eye: the dark pupil and the iris round it. The whole eyeball is about 8 mm across in the model and fills much of the head. Each eye points sideways, so the robin sees a wide area at once, and it turns its head to look at things with both eyes.
layers.deeper: The cut-open view shows the layers: the cornea, the iris, the lens, the vitreous, the retina, and the pecten, a pleated fold that is only found in birds. Click the retina to look inside it.
layers.expert: The eye is drawn about 8 mm across; the real size varies by individual. The visible dark dome in the plumage is the cornea and pupil; the iris is dark brown to black in a robin.

title: Eye ring
summary: A thin pale ring round the eye: the rim of the eyelids with a ring of tiny feathers.

layers.basics: Many birds have a ring round the eye, made of the eyelid rim and small feathers. In a robin it is faint.
layers.deeper: The ring follows the edge of the eyelids, which close over the eye.
layers.expert: The ring follows the edge of the eyelids. The model draws it as a thin tube; in life it is graded and feathered.

facts: round the eye, on the edge of the eyelids

title: Wing: the arm that became a wing
summary: A bird's wing is an arm: the same bones as ours, with the wrist and hand fused and the fingers reduced, and feathers in place of skin.

layers.basics: Fold your arm and compare. The wing has an upper arm bone (humerus), two forearm bones (radius and ulna), and a hand. The wrist and hand bones are fused into one hand bone, and only three fingers remain, one of them carrying the alula. The big feathers are attached to the forearm and hand bones. Use the "Cut open: the wing" view to see the bones and compare them with the human arm.
layers.deeper: Bones and muscles are the same family as ours; evolution kept the pattern and changed the proportions. The primaries are attached to the hand, the secondaries to the forearm, the tertials near the elbow; coverts overlay their roots. Muscles in the chest move the whole wing; very few muscles lie in the wing itself, which keeps the wing light.
layers.expert: Which three digits the bird hand keeps is debated: the fossils suggest I-II-III, the embryo II-III-IV. The model draws the bones of the folded wing in simplified form.

facts: 10 in most passerines, the outermost tiny (WFF, Pyle)
humerus, radius, ulna, fused hand bone, three fingers

ext.title: Pyle 2008: A molt primer for birders (Birding), feather tracts and counts

title: Primaries: the main flight feathers
summary: The primaries are the long flight feathers of the hand, the main thrust of a wing; most songbirds have ten, the outermost small.

layers.basics: These are the long, stiff feathers at the tip of the wing. They are attached to the hand and do most of the work of flying. A robin has ten, of which the outermost is tiny; the model draws all ten per wing, overlapping like the slats of a blind. Click one to read how it is built.
layers.deeper: Each feather has a central shaft, the rachis, with a flat vane on each side made of side branches (barbs), which carry smaller branches (barbules) with tiny hooks. The hooks fasten neighbouring barbs together like Velcro, so the vane is a smooth sheet that holds back most of the air. The base of the shaft, the hollow quill (calamus), sits in the skin and is anchored by ligaments to the bone.
layers.expert: Most modern passerines have ten primaries, and a few have only nine, lacking the tiny outer one. Each primary can be replaced in moult. The vane, rachis and barbules are made of beta-keratin.

facts: 10 in most modern passerines; the outermost is tiny
8 to 16 µm between neighbouring barbules on flight feathers of species from a hummingbird to a condor (J. R. Soc. Interface 2025)

ext.title: Pyle 2008: A molt primer for birders (Birding), feather tracts and counts
The feather's multi-functional structure across nano to macro scales inspires hierarchical design (J. R. Soc. Interface 22(225), 2025)

title: Secondaries
summary: The secondaries are the flight feathers of the forearm; a passerine has nine including three tertials.

layers.basics: The secondaries make up the inner part of the wing and form its broad surface. They are attached to the forearm bone, the ulna. A robin has nine in all, counting the three innermost ones, the tertials. The model draws six secondaries.
layers.deeper: The secondaries are attached to the ulna and stay close together in flight, so that together they make the curved airfoil shape of the wing. They tend to be shorter and broader than the primaries, with blunter tips.
layers.expert: In passerines the secondaries number nine counting the tertials; other birds range from six (hummingbirds) to as many as 40 (some albatrosses). Some authorities count only the three innermost, shorter and more symmetrical feathers as tertials; the model draws six secondaries and three tertials.

ext.title: Pyle 2008: A molt primer for birders (Birding), feather tracts and counts

title: Tertials
summary: The three innermost secondaries, which lie over the folded wing like a roof.

layers.basics: The tertials are the three feathers nearest the body, attached near the elbow. When the wing is folded they cover the bases of the primaries and the elbow.
layers.deeper: Technically the tertials are part of the secondary tract; they differ in having shafts set into the tissue near the elbow joint rather than into the ulna.
layers.expert: They are drawn shorter and broader than the other secondaries.

ext.title: Pyle 2008: A molt primer for birders (Birding), feather tracts and counts

title: Coverts: small feathers over the flight feathers
summary: The coverts are short feathers that cover the shafts of the flight feathers and smooth the wing surface; there are several rows.

layers.basics: Over the roots of the long feathers lie rows of shorter ones: the primary coverts, the greater, median and lesser coverts. They protect the shafts and smooth the airflow. In first-winter robins the tips of the coverts are yellow-brown and more obvious, which helps tell young birds from old.
layers.deeper: Coverts lie above and below the flight feathers: at least one layer on each side. In the model each of the four groups is drawn, from the long greater coverts to the small lesser coverts, as a set of overlapping blades.
layers.expert: The counts of coverts in each row are drawn to make the rows look right; they are not measured counts.

title: Alula
summary: The alula is a small group of feathers on the bird's "thumb", used like a slat on an aircraft wing for slow flight and landing.

layers.basics: The alula is a few small feathers at the front of the wrist. When a bird slows down to land, it lifts the alula and the air stays smoothly attached to the wing instead of breaking away. The model draws three.
layers.deeper: The alula is carried on the first digit of the hand, the "thumb" (which digits the bird hand keeps is debated: see the finger bones card). It is not counted as a true flight feather, but it is an aid to slow flight.
layers.expert: The comparison with a leading-edge slat on an aircraft wing is an analogy for the effect, not a measurement on a robin. The number of alula feathers varies by species; three are drawn.

facts: avoids stalling at low speed, as when landing

title: Rachis: the shaft of a feather
summary: The rachis is the stiff, tapering central shaft of a feather, with the vane growing out on each side.

layers.basics: The rachis runs the length of the feather. It is a light, springy rod that bends and springs back. Below the vane it becomes the hollow quill that fits into the skin.
layers.deeper: The barbs are fused to the rachis in a row on each side. The rachis is thickest at the base, where it is cylindrical and hollow, and tapers to the tip.
layers.expert: The shaft is made of beta-keratin, and its core carries bundles of 3 nm keratin filaments (J. R. Soc. Interface 2025). The model draws it as a thin tube scaled by the feather length.

title: Tail feathers (12)
summary: The tail is a fan of twelve long feathers, which steers and brakes the bird in flight.

layers.basics: Most passerines have twelve tail feathers, six on each side, and so does a robin. They are called rectrices (the singular is rectrix). The middle pair lies on top when the tail is closed. In flight the tail spreads to give lift and to steer. The feathers are anchored to the pygostyle, a small plate of fused tail bones.
layers.deeper: The tail feathers are held by a pad of muscle and fat at the base. Their count is not fixed in all birds: some passerines have 10, 8 or even 6, the superb lyrebird has 16.
layers.expert: In the model the tail is drawn closed, with twelve feathers lying in a slightly rounded fan.

ext.title: Pyle 2008: A molt primer for birders (Birding), feather tracts and counts

title: Tail coverts
summary: Short feathers that cover the roots of the tail feathers from above and below.

layers.basics: Over and under the base of the tail, rows of shorter feathers cover the roots of the twelve tail feathers. The upper ones are brown like the back; the under ones are pale buff.
layers.deeper: Like the wing coverts, they smooth the airflow and protect the shafts, with at least one layer above and below.
layers.expert: Two rows each are drawn; the number is approximate.

facts: upper and under, two drawn each

title: Shin (tibiotarsus)
summary: The lowest part of the shin, where the long leg bone comes out of the belly feathers.

layers.basics: The upper leg of a bird is hidden by the body feathers: the thigh bone and the knee are inside. What shows first is the shin, the tibiotarsus, which is the shin bone fused with some ankle bones. It is covered with a feathered or smooth skin that runs down to the ankle.
layers.deeper: The tibiotarsus is the longest leg bone of a robin. Its muscles, in the shin, sit high, close to the body, and long tendons run down to the toes, so the lower leg is light and thin.
layers.expert: The shape and length of the visible shin depend on how the belly feathers are fluffed.

facts: tibiotarsus: tibia fused with proximal tarsal bones

title: Ankle: the "backward knee"
summary: The joint that looks like a backward knee is the ankle; the real knee is hidden in the belly feathers.

layers.basics: The bend in a bird's leg that points backward is not the knee. It is the ankle (the heel). Birds walk on their toes, so their foot bones, the tarsus, are long and stand almost upright. The true knee is hidden in the feathers higher up and bends forward like yours.
layers.deeper: The ankle is the joint between the tibiotarsus and the tarsometatarsus. When a perching bird squats, bending the ankle tightens the toe-flexor tendon that runs behind it and curls the toes around the perch.
layers.expert: The ankle (intertarsal) joint is a hinge between the tibiotarsus and the tarsometatarsus, a joint found also in some reptiles. The model draws it as a small ball.

title: Tarsus: the scaly foot bone
summary: The tarsus is the long, scaly part of the leg, a foot bone that has become a leg segment.

layers.basics: What looks like the lower leg of a bird is part of its foot. The long, thin tarsus is the fused foot bones (the tarsometatarsus), covered in horny scales. It adds an extra segment to the leg and lengthens the stride.
layers.deeper: The tarsometatarsus is a segment specific to birds; it gives the leg extra lever length. A robin has long legs for a bird of its size and hops on the ground.
layers.expert: The tarsus is a straight rod with faint rings for the scales; real scales are in rows called scutes.

facts: tarsometatarsus: fused foot bones, specific to birds

title: Toes: three forward, one back
summary: A robin's foot has three toes pointing forward and one pointing back, the usual arrangement of a perching bird.

layers.basics: Three toes point forward and one, the hind toe or hallux, points back. This is the arrangement of nearly all songbirds and most other perching birds, called anisodactyl. The toes have 3, 4 and 5 bones in the inner, middle and outer front toes and 2 in the hind toe.
layers.deeper: On a branch, the toes close around the perch from front and back. In this model the bird stands on a boulder, so its toes are spread on the rock.
layers.expert: The toe bones number 3, 4, 5 and 2 in a typical perching bird. The model draws them with bones of that number.

facts: anisodactyl: toes II, III, IV forward, toe I back

title: Hind toe (hallux)
summary: The single toe pointing backward: the one that closes against the front toes in a perching grip.

layers.basics: The hind toe points backward and is the first toe, the equivalent of our big toe. It has two bones. On a perch it closes against the three front toes.
layers.deeper: The hallux is the same bone as the human big toe. In a perching bird it is on the opposite side of the foot from the three forward toes, which is what makes the grip a pincer.
layers.expert: Its claw is a keratin sheath over the last toe bone; the base of the hind toe is the unfused first metatarsal. The model draws it with a long curved claw, by eye.

title: Claws
summary: Each toe ends in a curved claw, a sheath of keratin over the last toe bone.

layers.basics: Each toe ends in a claw: a sheath of keratin over the last toe bone, strong enough to grip bark and rock. A human nail covers the end of a finger in the same way, but a claw curves round the toe.
layers.deeper: Bird claws, bills and the scales of the lower leg are all made of keratin; bird scales are beta-keratin, and some foot structures once thought to be scales are alpha-keratin. Claws grow and wear down in use.
layers.expert: The exact keratin type of a robin's claw is not stated: the Keratin page says beta-keratin is found in the feathers, beaks and claws of birds and reptiles, while alpha-keratin also occurs in birds. The curve in the model is drawn by eye.

facts: keratin over the last toe bone

title: Skin
summary: The robin's skin is thin and light, and bare between the feather tracts.

layers.basics: Under the feathers a bird's skin is thin. Feathers grow from small pits (follicles) in rows. Between the rows the skin is bare, which lets the feathers be raised and lowered by tiny muscles.
layers.deeper: Feathers, bill and claws are skin structures made of keratin, in the way that hair and nails are for us.
layers.expert: The model draws the skin as a thin shell. The real skin varies in thickness from place to place.

facts: feathers, bill sheath, claws, scales of the legs

title: Muscles
summary: The robin's muscles: the very large flight muscles of the breast, with smaller muscles in the neck, back, wing, tail and legs.

layers.basics: A flying bird puts most of its muscle in the breast, close to the centre of the body, so that the wings are light. Muscle drives everything the robin does: beating the wing, turning the head, hopping, and singing.
layers.deeper: Click a muscle to read what it does. The flight muscles are the pectoralis and supracoracoideus.
layers.expert: The muscle shapes are schematic, drawn as simple solids.

title: Soft tissue (a stand-in)
summary: In the cut view the pale pink between the organs is a stand-in for fat, connective tissue and the many small parts that are not drawn.

layers.basics: A real bird has no empty spaces inside: between the organs there are fat, connective tissue and fluid. In the cut-open view the model fills the gaps with a pale pink shape so that the cut looks solid. It is a drawing aid and not a tissue.
layers.deeper: The fill is a closed shape set a few millimetres inside the skin.
layers.expert: It carries no information about the real tissue.

title: Skeleton
summary: A bird's skeleton is light and fused: hollow bones, a keeled breastbone, a wishbone, a fused hand, a long neck.

layers.basics: The skeleton holds the robin up and gives the muscles something to pull on. In a bird many bones that are separate in us are fused: the hand, the hip and lower back, the tail tip. The breastbone carries a deep keel and the two collarbones are fused into a wishbone.
layers.deeper: Click a bone to read what it is and what it is in a human. Songbirds typically have a long neck of 14 vertebrae, no teeth, and ribs with small hooks. The skeleton is only about 5 % of a bird's body weight.
layers.expert: The bone shapes are drawn as simplified rods and plates.

ext.title: Webster and Goff: Variation in the vertebral column and ribs of songbirds (Proc. Indiana Acad. Sci.; 159 birds of 47 species)

title: Organs
summary: The robin's organs: heart, liver, stomach and gizzard, intestines, kidneys, eyes, with the lungs and air sacs shown separately.

layers.basics: Inside the body lie the heart, the liver, a two-part stomach, the intestines and the kidneys. A bird has no teeth and no bladder; it grinds food in a muscular stomach, the gizzard, and passes uric acid with its droppings through one opening, the cloaca.
layers.deeper: Click an organ to see what it is. The lungs and the air sacs are in their own layer.
layers.expert: Organ shapes, sizes and positions are approximate.

title: Pectoralis: the downstroke muscle
summary: The pectoralis is the robin's biggest muscle, a sheet over the breast that pulls the wing down.

layers.basics: The pectoralis lies on each side of the keel, over the ribs and the underside of the breast. When it contracts it pulls the wing down, and the downstroke makes most of the lift and thrust of a beat. This is why a bird has such a plump breast.
layers.deeper: The muscle runs from the keel and the wishbone to the humerus, on its crest. It is the muscle bird-lovers mean by "breast". It is made of fibres packed with mitochondria that supply the energy of flight; click the muscle's scene to look inside.
layers.expert: The pectoralis is the larger of the two flight muscles. It is drawn as a thick sheet over the sternum; its size is schematic.

title: Supracoracoideus: the upstroke muscle
summary: The supracoracoideus lies under the pectoralis, yet it lifts the wing, by pulling a tendon over the shoulder like a rope over a pulley.

layers.basics: It would be natural to put the muscle that lifts the wing on the bird's back, but the supracoracoideus lies on the breast, beside the keel, under the pectoralis. A long tendon runs from it up through a gap in the shoulder, the triosseal canal, and over the top to the humerus. The gap acts as a pulley: a pull down in the breast becomes a lift of the wing.
layers.deeper: The muscle is the smaller of the two flight muscles. Keeping both heavy muscles low in the body, near the centre of gravity, keeps the bird stable. This arrangement is a feature of modern birds; early birds such as Archaeopteryx may have lacked it.
layers.expert: The tendon passes through the triosseal canal, formed by the coracoid, the scapula and the wishbone. The canal is drawn as a small ring in the cut-open wing view.

facts: the triosseal canal at the shoulder

title: Tendon of the supracoracoideus
summary: The strong cord that carries the pull of the upstroke muscle over the shoulder to the top of the wing bone.

layers.basics: A tendon is a tough cord that joins muscle to bone. This one starts in the upstroke muscle on the breast, passes up through the shoulder pulley, and ends on the top of the humerus.
layers.deeper: Because the tendon is long and thin, the heavy muscle can stay low in the body while only a light cord runs to the wing.
layers.expert: The route is: muscle, through the triosseal canal (the gap between coracoid, scapula and furcula), and over the shoulder to the humerus. The model draws it as a thin tube along that route.

facts: supracoracoideus, triosseal canal, top of the humerus

title: Triosseal canal: the shoulder pulley
summary: A gap between three bones of the shoulder through which the upstroke tendon runs.

layers.basics: Three bones meet at the shoulder: the coracoid, the scapula and the wishbone. They leave a small opening, the triosseal canal. The tendon of the upstroke muscle runs through it, which turns a downward pull in the breast into an upward lift of the wing.
layers.deeper: The pulley lets both of the big flight muscles lie low on the breast, near the bird's centre of gravity. In most vertebrates the muscles that lift the arm lie on the back.
layers.expert: Attaching both muscles to the keel is unusual, because in other vertebrates the muscles that raise the upper limb are generally attached on the back. The ring in the model marks the canal and is simplified.

title: Neck, back and tail muscles
summary: Long muscles along the neck and back that hold the head and body steady, and a pair at the base of the tail.

layers.basics: Long muscles along the neck and back move the head and keep the trunk steady in flight; short, strong muscles at the base of the tail spread and steer the tail feathers.
layers.deeper: A bird's neck is long and flexible and its muscles do the jobs for the head that other animals do with their front limbs. The skin muscles also adjust the feathers.
layers.expert: The neck is long and has complex muscles, because the head does jobs that other animals do with their front limbs; the few trunk and tail muscles, such as the lateralis caudae and levator caudae, are strong and control the spreading of the tail feathers. The model draws simple tubes.

title: Jaw muscle
summary: The muscle that closes the lower jaw, a pad behind and below the eye.

layers.basics: The jaw muscle lies on the side of the head, behind the eye, and pulls the lower jaw shut. The muscles that close the jaws attach on the skull behind the eye.
layers.deeper: The muscles that move the jaws attach on the skull behind the eyes. A bird has no teeth to power, so the jaw muscles are small beside the flight muscles.
layers.expert: In birds the space for jaw muscles in the skull has been reduced. The model draws one ellipsoid on each side. Its mass is not stated.

title: Wing muscles
summary: Small, slim muscles in the upper and lower arm that fold and unfold the wing; the big ones are in the breast.

layers.basics: The wing has few muscles of its own: the big flight muscles are in the chest and long tendons run to the wing. Small muscles in the upper arm and forearm extend or fold the elbow, move the wing as a whole and move the fingers.
layers.deeper: Keeping muscle in the chest and not in the wing leaves the wing light, which makes flapping cheaper. Skin muscles attached to the feather bases adjust the feathers.
layers.expert: The wing muscles work mainly by straightening or bending the elbow, moving the whole wing, or straightening or bending particular fingers. The model draws two tapering muscle bellies on each side.

title: Thigh muscles
summary: The thick thigh muscles, inside the belly feathers, that swing the leg.

layers.basics: The thigh muscles are hidden under the belly feathers. They swing the leg for hopping and for take-off, and long tendons run from them down the leg to the toes.
layers.deeper: Putting the leg muscles high and close to the body leaves the lower leg thin and light, which is why a bird's leg looks so slim below the feathers.
layers.expert: The model draws one capsule from hip to knee. Its mass is not stated; in a bird the pectoral muscles are the largest muscles and the leg muscles are much smaller.

facts: hip to knee, hidden in the feathers

title: Shank muscles
summary: Muscles of the shin that move the foot by long tendons.

layers.basics: The muscles that curl the toes lie high on the shin, near the knee, so the lower leg can be thin. Their long tendons run down behind the ankle to the toes.
layers.deeper: The toe-flexor tendon is the one that tightens when the ankle bends, which helps a perching bird hold on (see the perching card).
layers.expert: The model draws one tapering capsule on the shin. Individual muscles are not drawn.

title: Tail muscles
summary: Small muscles at the root of the tail that spread, fold and tilt the tail feathers.

layers.basics: Small muscles at the root of the tail spread, fold and tilt the tail feathers. They pull on the pygostyle and on the feather bases.
layers.deeper: Two of them are the lateralis caudae and the levator caudae, which control the tail and spread the feathers, increasing the tail's area, which helps in turning.
layers.expert: The model draws two small ellipsoids. Their size and exact attachments are not described here.

title: Perching tendon
summary: A long tendon runs behind the ankle to the toes; bending the ankle tightens it and curls the toes without effort.

layers.basics: This is the tendon that makes a perch grip easy. It runs from the shin muscles, behind the ankle joint and down the back of the foot, where it splits to the toes. When the ankle bends, the tendon is stretched and pulls the toes shut. The tendon and the tissue around it are rough, so the grip holds until the leg straightens.
layers.deeper: Because the lock needs no continuous muscle effort, a bird can hold on while resting.
layers.expert: In the model the tendon is drawn with ridges where it passes the ankle, to stand for the rough surface; the real ridges and sheath are finer.

facts: shin muscle, behind the ankle, down the back of the foot, to the toes
open_questions: How much do birds rely on the lock while perching and sleeping? A study of starlings found sleeping birds did not bend the leg enough to engage it.

ext.title: Why don't birds fall off branches when they sleep (Science ABC)

title: Skull
summary: A light, toothless skull with huge eye sockets.

layers.basics: The skull is a thin shell of bone with no teeth, and the two eye sockets take up much of its side. The bill is the jaw bones sheathed in horn. A bird's skull weighs only about 1 % of its body weight.
layers.deeper: A bird skull is made of many small bones that do not overlap, like the juvenile skull of its dinosaur ancestors. The skull sits on the first neck vertebra by a single round knob (the occipital condyle), which lets the head turn far.
layers.expert: The skull has five major bones (frontal, parietal, premaxillary, nasal and the mandible) and the eye is ringed by small bones (the scleral ring). Birds have lost the bone behind the eye and the teeth. The model draws a smooth braincase with two sockets; the joints between the bones are not shown.

title: Upper jaw bone
summary: The bone inside the upper half of the bill: the premaxilla, with the horny sheath over it.

layers.basics: The upper bill has a bone core, the premaxilla, with a sheath of horn over it. The nostrils open at its base. In birds this one bone has grown large and become the upper bill, while the upper jaw bone behind it (the maxilla) is small.
layers.deeper: All living birds can move the upper jaw relative to the braincase (cranial kinesis); it is easiest to see in parrots. In sparrows the upper jaw rotates about a kinetic joint with the braincase (Hoese and Westneat 1996), so songbirds are not rigid-skulled. How far a robin's bill moves is not measured here.
layers.expert: The premaxilla has enlarged to form the bill while the maxilla has shrunk. The bill is covered by the rhamphotheca, a thin keratin layer. The model draws a thin cone, with no joint.

facts: upper jaw moves relative to the braincase in all living birds (cranial kinesis)

ext.title: Hoese and Westneat 1996: Biomechanics of cranial kinesis in birds: testing linkage models in the white-throated sparrow (J. Morphology 227: 305-320), abstract

title: Lower jaw bone
summary: The two-pronged bone of the lower bill, hinged on each side of the skull.

layers.basics: The lower jaw is made of two slender bones, joined at the tip, that hinge on the skull at the quadrate bones. A horny sheath covers it.
layers.deeper: In a human the lower jaw hinges straight on the skull; in a bird a separate bone, the quadrate, sits in the hinge. The quadrate also takes part in the movement of the upper bill, so opening the mouth and lifting the upper bill are linked.
layers.expert: The mandible is one of the five major bones of the skull. The model draws two thin rods. The link between quadrate and upper bill is part of cranial kinesis, which differs between groups.

facts: mandible, which hinges directly on the skull

title: Neck vertebrae (typically 14)
summary: A songbird's neck typically has 14 vertebrae, about twice as many as a person's seven.

layers.basics: A robin's neck is flexible because it is made of many small vertebrae: songbirds typically have 14, where a human has seven. It lets the bird reach its whole body with its bill to preen and turn its head far to look back.
layers.deeper: In a study of 159 birds of 47 songbird species, all but two had 14 neck vertebrae when the last two, which carry short floating ribs (cervico-dorsal vertebrae), were counted. Whether those two count as neck or back bones is a matter of convention, so published counts of 13 and 14 both exist; the robin itself is not named in the study.
layers.expert: Across all birds the count ranges from 8 to as many as 25 in some swans. The model draws 14 beads. The two floating ribs are not drawn. The count is therefore a typical songbird value, not a measurement of a robin.

facts: 14 in all but 2 of 159 birds of 47 species, counting 2 cervico-dorsal (Webster and Goff)

ext.title: Webster and Goff: Variation in the vertebral column and ribs of songbirds (Proc. Indiana Acad. Sci.; 159 birds of 47 species)

title: Chest vertebrae
summary: The chest vertebrae carry the ribs; in birds several of them are fused, so the back is stiff.

layers.basics: The vertebrae of the chest carry the ribs. In many birds the front ones are fused into a stiff block, so the body is a rigid frame that the wings can pull against.
layers.deeper: Birds have between five and ten thoracic vertebrae. The first thoracic vertebra is the one whose rib reaches the breastbone; the ribs of the neck vertebrae are free.
layers.expert: In the one house sparrow skeleton described by Webster and Goff the ribs that join the breastbone are on vertebrae 15 to 18; the robin was not measured. The model draws five beads and five pairs of ribs, a choice of the model.

facts: Ribs reaching the breastbone, house sparrow
4 (Webster and Goff); the robin was not measured

ext.title: Webster and Goff: Variation in the vertebral column and ribs of songbirds (Proc. Indiana Acad. Sci.; 159 birds of 47 species)

title: Synsacrum: the fused lower back and hip
summary: The lower back and hip bones are fused into one rigid piece, the synsacrum.

layers.basics: In a bird many vertebrae of the lower back and hip are fused into a single bone, the synsacrum, which is also fused to the hip bones. It makes a stiff, strong platform for the legs.
layers.deeper: The synsacrum is one piece made of thoracic, lumbar, sacral and sacro-caudal vertebrae. When the bird is not in flight it is the main support for the rest of the body. A human has a similar fused sacrum but only five vertebrae are fused in it.
layers.expert: The usual description of the fused synsacrum is one thoracic, six lumbar, two sacral and five sacro-caudal vertebrae fused, a general pattern for birds that is not measured on a robin; Webster and Goff report that the front part of the songbird synsacrum includes three or four thoraco-dorsal vertebrae, so the count varies. The model draws a tapering bar with a plate on each side.

facts: 1 thoracic + 6 lumbar + 2 sacral + 5 sacro-caudal (varies between birds)

ext.title: Webster and Goff: Variation in the vertebral column and ribs of songbirds (Proc. Indiana Acad. Sci.; 159 birds of 47 species)

title: Tail vertebrae
summary: A short chain of free tail bones between the hip and the pygostyle.

layers.basics: A bird has a short chain of free tail bones between the fused hip and the pygostyle. Birds have between five and eight free tail vertebrae; the robin's own number is not stated.
layers.deeper: These free vertebrae give the tail some movement near its root. They are the bird version of the human coccyx, the remains of a tail.
layers.expert: The model draws six beads, matching the six free tail vertebrae that Webster and Goff figure for a house sparrow; this is a drawing choice, not a count on a robin.

ext.title: Webster and Goff: Variation in the vertebral column and ribs of songbirds (Proc. Indiana Acad. Sci.; 159 birds of 47 species)

title: Pygostyle: the tail plate
summary: The last tail bones are fused into a small plate, the pygostyle, which holds the tail feathers.

layers.basics: Unlike a mammal, a bird has no long tail of bones. The last few tail vertebrae are fused into a flat plate called the pygostyle, and the tail feathers are fastened round it. The tail is feathers, not bone.
layers.deeper: The pygostyle gives the tail feathers and the small tail muscles a firm anchor, so the tail can be spread and tilted as one unit for steering.
layers.expert: The pygostyle is made of the last four caudal vertebrae, though some sources count up to ten. The model draws a small plate.

facts: the last four (up to ten by some counts)

title: Breastbone with its keel
summary: The breastbone carries a deep keel, a blade to which the flight muscles attach.

layers.basics: The sternum is a broad plate with a deep ridge down the middle, the keel, like the keel of a boat. The big flight muscles are attached on both sides of it. Flightless birds such as ostriches have no keel.
layers.deeper: A deeper keel gives the muscles more area to attach to. Flying birds have a sternum about as wide as it is tall, walking birds a long one and swimming birds a wide one.
layers.expert: The keel gives the muscles for flying or swimming a place to attach, and flightless birds such as ostriches lack a keel and have denser, heavier bones. The model draws the keel and plate smooth and oversized.

facts: carries the flight muscles; absent in ostriches

title: Wishbone (furcula)
summary: The two collarbones are fused into a V or U, the wishbone, which springs as the wings beat.

layers.basics: A bird's collarbones are joined into one bone, the furcula or wishbone, a V or U-shaped bone at the front of the chest. Birds are the only living vertebrates with fused collarbones. It lies between the two shoulders and holds them apart.
layers.deeper: A human has two separate collarbones. In the bird the wishbone also forms one side of the shoulder pulley (see Triosseal canal).
layers.expert: The wishbone and the coracoid, with the scapula, form the pectoral girdle. The wishbone is homologous to the fused clavicles of theropod dinosaurs, which is one of the features that link birds to them. The model draws a U.

facts: only in living birds (among living vertebrates)

title: Coracoids and shoulder blades
summary: The coracoid is a strong strut from the shoulder to the breastbone; the shoulder blade is a slender blade along the ribs.

layers.basics: The coracoid is a strong strut from the shoulder to the breastbone, and the shoulder blade (scapula) is a long, thin blade that lies along the ribs. With the wishbone they hold the shoulder joint and form the pulley for the upstroke tendon.
layers.deeper: In a human the coracoid is only a small hook on the shoulder blade, and the collarbone braces the shoulder. In the bird the coracoid is a full bone that takes the force of the wing beat.
layers.expert: The furcula, coracoid and scapula together make up the pectoral girdle. The model draws the coracoid and scapula as rods. The pulley they form is described on the Triosseal canal card.

facts: scapula (shoulder blade); the human coracoid is a small process on it

title: Ribs and their hooks
summary: The ribs have small hooks, the uncinate processes, that overlap the next rib and stiffen the cage.

layers.basics: The ribs form a stiff cage round the lungs, heart and liver. Each has a small bony hook, the uncinate process, that overlaps the rib behind it.
layers.deeper: Birds are the only living animals with bony uncinate processes of this kind, though the tuatara also has them. They strengthen the cage and anchor muscles used in breathing.
layers.expert: In the house sparrow in Webster and Goff the uncinate processes lie on ribs 14 to 18, which is not a robin count. The model draws five pairs of ribs and the real number varies.

ext.title: Webster and Goff: Variation in the vertebral column and ribs of songbirds (Proc. Indiana Acad. Sci.; 159 birds of 47 species)

title: Uncinate processes
summary: Little bony hooks on the ribs.

layers.basics: Each rib carries a small backward hook of bone that lies over the next rib. Together the hooks stiffen the rib cage so that it can take the pull of the muscles that work the breathing.
layers.deeper: They are hooked extensions of bone that overlap the rib behind. They are found in birds and in the tuatara, not in mammals.
layers.expert: They begin as cartilage and turn to bone in birds; in crocodiles they stay cartilage. The model draws short rods on five pairs of ribs.

title: Pelvis
summary: The hip bones are fused to the lower back; the joint for the leg is in the middle of the side.

layers.basics: The three hip bones (ilium, ischium and pubis) are fused into one on each side and to the synsacrum. The socket for the thigh bone, the acetabulum, is where they meet.
layers.deeper: In a human the two hip bones close in front to form a bowl that holds organs. The bird pelvis is not closed in a bowl in the same way.
layers.expert: The fused bones (the innominate bone) are important in evolution because the open, fused pelvis lets birds lay eggs. The model draws plates, not the real shapes.

title: Humerus: the upper arm
summary: The upper arm bone of the wing, the same bone as in your upper arm.

layers.basics: The humerus runs from the shoulder to the elbow. It is the bone you feel in your upper arm, and a bird's is light because many bird bones are hollow and braced with struts. In a folded wing it lies back along the body.
layers.deeper: The tendon of the upstroke muscle ends on its upper end, and the big breast muscle pulls on a crest of the bone. Whether a robin's humerus is air-filled is not stated: it is the bone shown in the hollow-bone scene as a general picture.
layers.expert: The shoulder is made of the scapula, coracoid and humerus, and the humerus meets the radius and ulna at the elbow. The model draws a rod with swollen ends.

title: Radius and ulna
summary: The radius, the thinner of the two forearm bones, beside the ulna.

layers.basics: The wing's forearm has two bones, the radius and the ulna, as yours does. The radius is the slimmer one and lies on the front edge of the wing.
layers.deeper: In a human the radius is the forearm bone on the thumb side. The secondary flight feathers attach to the ulna, not the radius.
layers.expert: The model draws two thin rods, the radius the slimmer; the real thicknesses are not stated.

ext.title: Pyle 2008: A molt primer for birders (Birding), feather tracts and counts

title: Ulna
summary: The thicker forearm bone, with the secondary feathers attached.

layers.basics: The ulna is the larger forearm bone. The secondary flight feathers are attached along it, so it carries most of the broad inner part of the wing.
layers.deeper: The tertials, the three feathers nearest the body, are attached close to the elbow. In a human the ulna is the forearm bone on the little-finger side.
layers.expert: The attachment of the secondaries to the ulna is described in Pyle 2008 and the Flight feather page. The model draws a rod; the small bumps where real feather bases attach are not drawn.

ext.title: Pyle 2008: A molt primer for birders (Birding), feather tracts and counts

title: Fused hand bone (carpometacarpus)
summary: The wrist and palm bones are fused into one hand bone that carries the primary flight feathers.

layers.basics: In your hand the wrist has eight small bones and the palm has five long bones. In a bird the wrist and palm bones are fused into one bone, the carpometacarpus, which carries the main flight feathers (the primaries).
layers.deeper: The fusion makes a stiff, light support for the long feathers. A few small wrist bones stay free, as in the bird's two bones at the wrist joint (the radiale and ulnare).
layers.expert: The wrist and palm bones form the bird's wrist and hand, and the finger bones are fused together. The model draws the carpometacarpus as one rod and the free wrist bones are not drawn. The statement that two wrist bones stay free is general anatomy of birds and not checked on a robin.

facts: wrist bones (carpals) and palm bones (metacarpals), partly fused in the bird

title: Finger bones and the alular digit
summary: Only three fingers remain; the "thumb" carries the alula.

layers.basics: A bird's hand has three digits. The short thumb carries the alula, and the longest finger holds the outer primary feathers. Which three of the original five digits these are is still debated.
layers.deeper: The fossils of theropod dinosaurs suggest digits I, II and III, while the embryos of living birds suggest II, III and IV. This is one of the real open problems in the origin of birds.
layers.expert: This difference is called the frame-shift question and is listed among the debated points in Origin of birds. The model draws two thin rods and a stub; the identity of the digits is not shown.

facts: debated: I-II-III from fossils, II-III-IV from embryos
open_questions: Which digits does the bird hand keep: I-II-III (fossils) or II-III-IV (embryos)?

title: Leg bones: femur, tibiotarsus, fibula, tarsometatarsus
summary: A bird's leg has three long segments: the thigh bone hidden in the body, the shin bone, and a foot bone that stands up as what looks like a lower leg.

layers.basics: The thigh bone (femur) is hidden in the belly feathers; below the knee come the shin bone (tibiotarsus) with a thin splint (fibula), and then the tarsometatarsus, a long foot bone. The bend you can see in a bird's leg is the ankle, between the shin bone and that foot bone. Click each bone for its own card.
layers.deeper: A person has a thigh bone, two shin bones, a set of small ankle bones and five long foot bones. In the bird the upper ankle bones have fused onto the shin bone and the long foot bones have fused into one, which adds a third long segment that humans do not have. The toes then follow.
layers.expert: The bones of the lower leg are the tibiotarsus (the tibia with the upper foot bones fused onto it) and the tarsometatarsus (the lower foot bones merged with metatarsals II, III and IV), and the first metatarsal stays separate as the base of the hind toe. The leg bones are the heaviest of a bird's skeleton, which keeps its centre of gravity low. The model draws all four as plain rods.

facts: thigh (femur), shin (tibiotarsus, with the fibula), foot bone (tarsometatarsus), toes
femur, tibia and fibula, ankle and foot bones; the bird fuses several of them

title: Thigh bone (femur)
summary: The thigh bone, from the hip socket to the knee, hidden inside the body feathers.

layers.basics: The femur runs from the hip socket in the fused pelvis to the knee. The knee points forward, as yours does, but it is hidden in the feathers, so the joint you see bending backward lower down is the ankle and not the knee.
layers.deeper: This is the same bone as the human thigh bone. At the knee it meets the tibiotarsus and the fibula. Because it sits inside the body outline, a robin looks as if its leg starts at the belly.
layers.expert: The femur fits into the hip socket (acetabulum), where the ilium, ischium and pubis meet; in some flightless birds (ostrich, emu) the femur is hollow and air-filled, but this is not stated for songbirds. The model draws it as a rod whose length and angle are chosen by eye.

facts: joins the tibiotarsus and fibula; the knee points forward, hidden in feathers

title: Shin bone (tibiotarsus)
summary: The shin bone: the tibia fused with the upper ankle bones, the longest bare-looking segment of the leg.

layers.basics: The tibiotarsus is a bird's shin bone. Its name says what it is: the tibia fused with the upper bones of the ankle. At its top, next to the knee, it has a raised ridge called the cnemial crest.
layers.deeper: In a human the shin bone is the tibia alone, and the ankle is a cluster of separate small bones below it. In the robin those upper ankle bones are part of the shin bone, so the ankle joint lies at the bottom of the tibiotarsus, between it and the foot bone.
layers.expert: The upper foot bones are fused onto the tibia, and one set of ankle bones (the centralia) is missing altogether. The ankle joint within the tarsus is also found in some reptiles. The model draws the bone as a rod with no crest.

facts: tibia fused with the upper ankle bones
tibia (shin bone); the ankle bones are separate in a human

title: Fibula
summary: The thin bone that lies against the shin bone; in birds it is much reduced.

layers.basics: Birds have a fibula, but it is a thin splint pressed against the shin bone. It runs alongside the tibiotarsus for part of its length and does not reach the ankle.
layers.deeper: In a human the fibula is a slender but complete bone beside the tibia, reaching the ankle. In most birds it has shrunk, and only penguins keep a full-length one. Birds put the strength of the lower leg into the one fused shin bone.
layers.expert: The fibula is reduced and stuck to the tibia, and usually runs about two thirds of its length; only penguins keep a full-length fibula. The model draws a thin rod beside the shin bone, which is hard to click for that reason.

facts: usually about two thirds of the shin bone
fibula, which is complete in a human

title: Foot bone (tarsometatarsus)
summary: The long, upright foot bone: a segment of leg found only in birds, which gives the leg its extra lever length.

layers.basics: What looks like a robin's lower leg is really part of its foot. The long bone, the tarsometatarsus, stands upright, and the bird walks on its toes. It is covered with scales and no feathers.
layers.deeper: A human foot has seven ankle bones and five long foot bones that lie flat on the ground. In the bird the lower ankle bones and three of the long foot bones have fused into one bone, which stands up and adds a whole extra segment to the leg. This lengthens the leg like a longer lever.
layers.expert: The tarsometatarsus is made of the lower ankle bones merged with metatarsals II, III and IV, and metatarsal I stays separate as the base of the hind toe. Most birds are digitigrade, walking on the toes. Scales of the bare lower leg are keratin. The model draws the bone as a rod.

facts: lower ankle bones and metatarsals II, III and IV fused
ankle and long foot bones, which stay separate in a human

title: Toe bones
summary: The toes have 3, 4 and 5 bones in the three front toes and 2 in the hind toe.

layers.basics: Each toe is a chain of small bones: three in the inner front toe, four in the middle one, five in the outer one, and two in the hind toe. The last bone of each toe carries the claw.
layers.deeper: A human big toe has two bones and the other toes three; the robin's hind toe (the hallux) matches the big toe and also has two. The extra bones in the outer front toes make them longer and more flexible, which helps them close round a perch.
layers.expert: The 3, 4, 5, 2 pattern is stated for a typical perching bird, not measured on a robin; the hallux is the same bone as the human big toe. The model draws the bones in that number as short rods.

facts: toe bones; the hind toe matches the big toe

title: Heart
summary: A four-chambered heart, large and fast for the bird's size, that pumps blood to the flight muscles.

layers.basics: The heart has four chambers: two atria that receive blood and two ventricles that pump it. The right side sends blood to the lungs; the left side sends it round the body, and the two sides do not mix. Use "Cut open: the heart" to see the chambers.
layers.deeper: Oxygen-poor blood enters the right atrium, passes to the right ventricle and goes to the lungs; it returns to the left atrium and is pumped by the left ventricle round the body. The wall of the left ventricle is the thickest. The animation is an illustration with no real rate.
layers.expert: A four-chambered heart is shared with mammals and crocodilians. A small tropical songbird of 17 g in the wild ranged from 260 to 824 beats a minute (Steiger et al. 2009); no heart rate was measured on a robin. The model heart has no valves.

ext.title: Steiger et al. 2009: Heart-rate telemetry of a small tropical bird, the spotted antbird (Physiol. Biochem. Zool.)

title: Left ventricle
summary: The thick-walled chamber that pumps oxygen-rich blood round the whole body.

layers.basics: The left ventricle receives blood that has been to the lungs and pumps it to the body through the main artery (the aorta). Its wall is the thickest in the heart.
layers.deeper: The main artery (the aorta) leaves the heart and curves to the body.
layers.expert: The cavity is drawn as an ellipsoid inside the heart muscle; the valves are not drawn. The thicker wall is the standard description of the bird heart and no wall thickness is given .

title: Right ventricle
summary: The chamber that pumps oxygen-poor blood to the lungs.

layers.basics: The right ventricle wraps round part of the left one and sends oxygen-poor blood to the lungs. Its wall is thinner than that of the left ventricle, because the lung circuit needs less pressure than the body circuit.
layers.deeper: In the bird the right ventricle is crescent-shaped when cut across. Blood leaves it by the pulmonary artery to the lungs.
layers.expert: The crescent in the model follows the usual drawing of a bird heart; the real wall thickness is not stated.

title: Left atrium
summary: The small chamber that receives oxygen-rich blood from the lungs.

layers.basics: The left atrium receives oxygen-rich blood from the lungs and passes it to the left ventricle. Its wall is thin.
layers.deeper: It is the same chamber as the human left atrium.
layers.expert: The atria are thin-walled receiving chambers. The model draws a small ellipsoid; the valve between atrium and ventricle is not drawn.

title: Right atrium
summary: The small chamber that receives oxygen-poor blood from the body.

layers.basics: The right atrium receives oxygen-poor blood from the body and passes it to the right ventricle. Its wall is thin.
layers.deeper: In chickens and some other birds the great vein that brings blood from the upper body is double, so there are two openings into the right atrium instead of one.
layers.expert: In chickens the great vein from the upper body is double. Whether a robin's is double is not stated. The model draws one ellipsoid.

title: Liver
summary: The liver, a large two-lobed organ behind the heart.

layers.basics: The liver is the largest gland of the body. It makes bile, which helps digest fat, stores sugar and cleans the blood. In birds it has two lobes.
layers.deeper: It lies just behind the heart, in front of the stomach.
layers.expert: The model draws two lobes, the right slightly bigger. Their size is drawn by eye; the liver's mass is not stated.

title: Gullet (oesophagus), and the crop question
summary: The tube from the throat to the stomach. Many birds have a crop on it; the model does not draw one on the robin.

layers.basics: Food goes from the throat to the stomach down the gullet, behind the windpipe. In many birds a crop, a muscular pouch, softens and stores food on the way. The model draws the gullet as a tube without a crop.
layers.deeper: A crop is an enlarged part of the oesophagus, and not all birds have one. Doves and pigeons make crop milk in it to feed their young.
layers.expert: In the model the robin's gullet is a tube without a crop; that is a modelling choice. Anatomy texts differ on whether songbirds have a true crop or only a slight widening of the gullet, and a robin was not checked.

facts: present in many birds, absent in owls; not drawn here for the robin

title: Proventriculus: the glandular stomach
summary: The first of the bird's two stomachs: it adds acid and enzymes.

layers.basics: A bird's stomach has two parts. The first, the proventriculus, makes the digestive juices: hydrochloric acid and the enzyme pepsin. The second part is the muscular gizzard.
layers.deeper: The proventriculus is a short tube between the gullet and the gizzard that secretes hydrochloric acid and pepsinogen; the acid turns pepsinogen into pepsin, which cuts proteins into peptides. The juices are mixed with the food by the gizzard's contractions.
layers.expert: This is the general bird pattern; the model draws a small oval in the place where the glandular stomach lies.

title: Gizzard: the muscular stomach
summary: The gizzard is the muscle that grinds food, doing the work of teeth.

layers.basics: Birds have no teeth; they grind food in the gizzard, a thick-walled muscular stomach. Some birds swallow grit to help.
layers.deeper: The gizzard is made of four muscular bands that rotate and crush the food, passing it from one area to another. In seed-eating birds such as turkeys and quails it holds swallowed grit or stone, called gastroliths. Whether a robin keeps grit is not stated.
layers.expert: Gastroliths have also been found as trace fossils with other dinosaurs, so using gizzard stones is a similarity between birds and some dinosaurs; it is not a feature of every theropod. The model draws a rounded disc.

facts: swallowed by some birds (not stated for the robin)

title: Spleen
summary: A small dark organ beside the stomach that handles blood and immune cells.

layers.basics: The spleen is a small round organ near the stomach. It filters the blood and is part of the immune system, which makes and stores immune cells.
layers.deeper: Birds also have an immune organ at the cloaca, the bursa of Fabricius, which helps make B lymphocytes.
layers.expert: The model draws a small ball next to the stomach; its size is drawn by eye.

title: Pancreas
summary: A thin gland that lies in the loop of the first part of the gut and makes digestive enzymes and hormones.

layers.basics: The pancreas makes digestive enzymes that go into the gut and hormones such as insulin and glucagon. In a bird it hangs between the limbs of the first loop of the small intestine (the duodenum).
layers.deeper: Compared with a mammal, a bird's blood sugar is high and its pancreas makes much more glucagon, which raises blood sugar, than insulin. Birds do not use glucose to trigger insulin release in the same way.
layers.expert: Birds keep higher blood glucose than other vertebrates of similar size (Braun and Sweazea 2008), and a later review puts it at nearly double that of mammals of similar size. A figure of 150 to 300 % higher in one encyclopedia page is not confirmed here. These are general bird values, not measured on a robin.

facts: higher than in mammals of similar size; nearly double in one review
between the limbs of the duodenum

ext.title: Braun and Sweazea 2008: Glucose regulation in birds (Comp. Biochem. Physiol. B 151: 1-9), abstract

title: Intestines and rectum
summary: The gut tube coils in the belly and ends in a short rectum and the cloaca.

layers.basics: Food passes from the gizzard along the small intestine, where it is digested and absorbed, to a short large intestine and the cloaca. A bird's gut is short, which keeps its weight down.
layers.deeper: Enzymes from the pancreas and the intestine finish the digestion, and the products are absorbed into the blood. Many birds regurgitate undigested hard bits as pellets, but not through the cloaca.
layers.expert: The model draws a coiled tube; the real gut is more folded. The shortness of a bird's gut is a general description in the Bird anatomy page.

title: Rectum
summary: The last short piece of the gut.

layers.basics: The rectum is the last short piece of the gut. It opens into the cloaca.
layers.deeper: Droppings and the white uric-acid paste of the urine leave together through the cloaca. In some birds urine from the cloaca is also moved back into the rectum.
layers.expert: Bird anatomy says urine from the kidney reaches the cloaca by the ureters and then back up into the colon. The model draws a short tube.

title: Cloaca: one opening for everything
summary: Gut, kidneys and reproductive organs all open into one chamber, the cloaca.

layers.basics: A bird has one exit for droppings, urine, eggs and sperm. The white part of a dropping is uric acid, the waste of the nitrogen in the diet, and it needs little water to get rid of.
layers.deeper: The urine is formed by the kidneys and goes down the ureters into the cloaca. A young bird has a pouch on the top of the cloaca, the bursa of Fabricius, which helps make B lymphocytes, a kind of immune cell.
layers.expert: In most male birds there is no penis; the sperm is passed when the two cloacae touch. This is the general bird pattern. The model draws a small chamber.

title: Kidneys
summary: Two kidneys, in hollows under the fused lower back, that clean the blood and make uric acid.

layers.basics: The two kidneys filter waste from the blood and lie on either side of the backbone against the lower back and pelvis. Birds pass their nitrogen waste as uric acid.
layers.deeper: Each kidney has three sections. Birds have two kinds of nephron (the filtering unit), one like a reptile's and one like a mammal's. There is no bladder; urine goes to the cloaca.
layers.expert: The concentration gradient in the avian kidney is made by salt and not by urea, as it is in mammals. The model draws three lobes on each side.

title: Eyeballs
summary: The two eyeballs, each about 8 mm across in the model, set in sockets at the sides of the skull.

layers.basics: The two eyeballs fill a large part of the head. Each eye has a cornea, a lens and a retina, and in a bird a small pleated organ, the pecten, projects into the jelly from the point where the optic nerve enters. Use "Cut open: the eye" to look inside one.
layers.deeper: A ring of small bones in the front of the eye supports its shape. Birds have the largest eyes for their body size of any animals, though much of the eye is hidden in the skull, and eye movements are small, so birds turn the head instead.
layers.expert: The eye is drawn about 8 mm across by eye from the head proportions; it is not a measured value.

title: Lungs
summary: The lungs are small, spongy and fixed against the ribs; they do not expand, the air sacs move the air.

layers.basics: A bird's lungs are small and firm, pressed against the back of the rib cage. They do not swell and shrink: the air sacs do the pumping. Gas exchange takes place in tiny tubes, the parabronchi, through which the air flows one way.
layers.deeper: The lungs are smaller than a mammal's of the same body mass, yet the respiratory surface is larger and the barrier between air and blood is thinner. Blood flows across the parabronchi at right angles to the air, a cross-current arrangement.
layers.expert: Birds have a respiratory surface about 15 % greater, a capillary blood volume 2.5 to 3 times larger and a blood-gas barrier 56 to 67 % thinner than in a mammal of similar mass, as general figures for birds, not a robin measurement. The lung is drawn as a wedge on each side of the spine.

ext.title: Airflow through the avian respiratory system, a tracer-gas study of zebra finches and blackbirds (open-access paper)

title: Air sacs
summary: Thin-walled air sacs fill much of the body and work as bellows, so that air flows through the lung in one direction.

layers.basics: Air sacs are thin bags among the organs, and some enter the bones. They act as bellows: fresh air goes first into the rear sacs, then through the lungs, then to the front sacs and out. A bird typically has nine; in passerines the clavicular sac may be joined to the anterior thoracic sacs, so passerines are counted as having seven.
layers.deeper: The sacs are in two groups: the front group (interclavicular, cervical and anterior thoracic) and the rear group (posterior thoracic and abdominal). The sac walls have a poor blood supply, so no gas exchange happens in them. The air sacs account for about 15 % of the body volume, where the alveoli of a mammal lung take about 7 %.
layers.expert: The count is a naming convention, not an unknown: nine is the textbook count of five groups (1 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 2), and passerines are counted as having seven because the clavicular air sacs may be joined to or fused with the anterior thoracic sacs. In some authors' names the interclavicular sac is the clavicular sac and the anterior and posterior thoracic sacs are the cranial and caudal thoracic sacs; a zebra finch has seven or eight. The model draws nine so that each group can be clicked. The count can range from seven to twelve across birds.

facts: seven, because the clavicular and anterior thoracic sacs may be fused

ext.title: Airflow through the avian respiratory system, a tracer-gas study of zebra finches and blackbirds (open-access paper)
