title: Interclavicular air sac
summary: The single air sac in the middle of the chest, in the front group of sacs.

layers.basics: This is the interclavicular sac, the one air sac that is not paired; it lies in the middle of the front of the chest between the collarbones. It belongs to the front group of sacs, which empty out through the windpipe.
layers.deeper: It is one of three anterior sacs (interclavicular, cervical and anterior thoracic). In passerines the interclavicular, or clavicular, sac may be joined or fused with the anterior thoracic sacs, which is one reason the number of sacs in a songbird is given as seven.
layers.expert: The model draws it as a single smooth bag in the front of the chest. Where its walls end and a neighbour begins is a drawing choice.

facts: may be fused with the anterior thoracic sacs

ext.title: Airflow through the avian respiratory system, a tracer-gas study of zebra finches and blackbirds (open-access paper)

title: Cervical air sacs
summary: A pair of air sacs at the base of the neck, in the front group.

layers.basics: The cervical sacs are small sacs at the base of the neck. They belong to the front group of air sacs, which fill with air that has already passed through the lungs and empty out through the windpipe.
layers.deeper: Air sacs form air pockets inside the semi-hollow bones in many birds, so a sac at the base of the neck can reach the neck vertebrae; which bones a robin's sacs enter is not stated. The sacs have poor blood supply and so do not exchange gas themselves.
layers.expert: The model draws two small bags. Whether a robin has separate cervical sacs is part of the naming and counting convention explained on the Air sacs card.

facts: none: the walls have a poor blood supply

ext.title: Airflow through the avian respiratory system, a tracer-gas study of zebra finches and blackbirds (open-access paper)

title: Anterior thoracic air sacs
summary: A pair of air sacs in the front of the chest, in the front group.

layers.basics: The anterior thoracic sacs lie in the front of the chest. They are part of the front group: on breathing out they release air that has already crossed the lung and send it up the windpipe.
layers.deeper: During inhalation both groups of sacs expand: the posterior sacs fill with fresh air, and the anterior sacs fill with air that has already passed through the lungs. In songbirds these sacs may be joined with the clavicular sac.
layers.expert: The model draws two bags. The fusion with the interclavicular sac in passerines is one reason textbooks differ on the count.

facts: fill with air that has already passed through the lungs

ext.title: Airflow through the avian respiratory system, a tracer-gas study of zebra finches and blackbirds (open-access paper)

title: Posterior thoracic air sacs
summary: A pair of air sacs in the rear of the chest, in the rear group, that take fresh air first.

layers.basics: The posterior thoracic sacs lie in the rear of the chest. They belong to the rear group, which fills with fresh air when the bird breathes in and empties it forward through the lungs when the bird breathes out.
layers.deeper: This is the step that keeps the flow through the lung going one way. The air that leaves a rear sac enters the lung from the rear end and flows through the parabronchi in the same direction as on the way in.
layers.expert: The model draws two bags. The tracer-gas study of zebra finches and blackbirds found the details of the flow differ from the simple textbook pattern (Airflow through the avian respiratory system).

ext.title: Airflow through the avian respiratory system, a tracer-gas study of zebra finches and blackbirds (open-access paper)

title: Abdominal air sacs
summary: A pair of large air sacs among the gut, at the rear of the body.

layers.basics: The abdominal sacs are the rearmost air sacs, lying among the gut inside the belly. They are in the rear group: they fill with fresh air on breathing in and push it through the lungs on breathing out.
layers.deeper: Birds have no diaphragm; they change the volume of all their air sacs together by moving the ribs and the belly wall. Breathing out is the active phase.
layers.expert: The model draws two large bags. Real sac shapes are more irregular and wrap round neighbouring organs.

facts: rib and belly muscles; birds have no diaphragm

ext.title: Airflow through the avian respiratory system, a tracer-gas study of zebra finches and blackbirds (open-access paper)

title: Windpipe (trachea)
summary: The windpipe is a tube of rings from the throat to the syrinx, deep in the chest.

layers.basics: The windpipe carries air from the throat to the lungs, down the front of the neck. It is held open by rings of cartilage. At its lower end it splits in two at the syrinx.
layers.deeper: A bird's windpipe is dead space: the oxygen-poor air in it at the end of a breath is the first air to re-enter the lungs and air sacs. In a bird this dead space is on average 4.5 times larger than in a mammal of the same size.
layers.expert: The tracheal rings are mostly complete rings, and the bronchi have C-shaped rings. The model draws a smooth tube; the rings show in the cut-open syrinx.

title: Brain
summary: The brain: a smooth, small brain with large optic lobes.

layers.basics: Much of the bird brain deals with sight: the optic lobes at the sides are large because vision matters to a bird. The cerebellum at the back helps control balance and movement.
layers.deeper: A bird has a large brain for its body mass, and its surface is smooth, without the deep folds of a human brain.
layers.expert: The brain is drawn by eye from a typical songbird brain. Its mass and the sizes of its parts are not stated; Only a large brain-to-body-mass ratio is stated for birds in general: a large brain-to-body-mass ratio.

title: Optic lobes
summary: The parts of the brain that receive signals from the eyes.

layers.basics: The optic lobes are two bulges at the sides of the midbrain. They receive most of the signals from the optic nerves, and they are large in birds.
layers.deeper: They are the bird's main visual centre in the midbrain, and are called the optic tectum. The visual centres in a mammal's cerebral cortex do much of the same work.
layers.expert: The model draws two ellipsoids. The sizes are drawn by eye. This card does not give a measured size for a robin.

facts: the optic tectum is the superior colliculus in mammals

title: Optic nerves
summary: The cables that carry signals from each eye to the brain.

layers.basics: Each optic nerve leaves the back of the eye and runs to the brain. It carries the signals of all the retina's ganglion cells.
layers.deeper: Birds have a high number of neurons in the optic nerve, which is one reason their eyesight is acute. In a bird the nerve leaves the eye where the pecten stands.
layers.expert: The model draws two thin cables. In a human the optic nerve also leaves at a blind spot with no photoreceptors, the optic disc.

title: Spinal cord
summary: The spinal cord runs from the brain through the vertebrae to the tail.

layers.basics: The spinal cord runs from the brain down through a canal in the vertebrae. It carries signals between the brain and the body, and nerves leave it between the vertebrae to the wings, legs and muscles.
layers.deeper: In a bird the neck part is long and the part in the fused back is held in a rigid canal. The cord ends in the tail region.
layers.expert: The model draws a tube. Its length and the places where nerves leave are not drawn from a dissection.

title: Nerves of the wing and the leg, and the vagus
summary: Nerves branch from the spinal cord to the wings and legs; the vagus nerves run between the brain and the heart and gut.

layers.basics: Nerves branch from the spinal cord to the wings and legs, and the vagus nerves run between the brain and the chest and gut. Click one of the three nerve cards for its job.
layers.deeper: The wing is supplied through a bundle called the brachial plexus. The leg is supplied by the sciatic nerve, and the vagus supplies the organs of the chest and belly.
layers.expert: The model draws thin cables of three kinds; the real branching is far more complex. There is no separate card for that nerve in the human body, so the human match is the general Peripheral nerves card.

ext.title: The Avian-RUM block: an anatomical cadaveric study of wing nerves in birds (Animals 2026)

title: Wing nerves (brachial plexus)
summary: The bundle of nerves that supplies the wing, branching from the spinal cord near the shoulder.

layers.basics: The nerves to the wing come from a network near the shoulder called the brachial plexus. Its branches carry movement commands to the wing muscles and bring back touch signals from the wing.
layers.deeper: In birds the forelimb is mostly supplied by two nerves, the radial nerve and the median-ulnar nerve, which are main branches of the plexus. Humans also have a brachial plexus, supplying the arm.
layers.expert: The branching pattern differs between bird species. Which spinal nerves form the plexus in a robin is not stated. There is no separate card for that nerve in the human body, so the human match is the general Peripheral nerves card.

facts: radial and median-ulnar nerves (birds in general)

ext.title: The Avian-RUM block: an anatomical cadaveric study of wing nerves in birds (Animals 2026)

title: Leg nerve (sciatic)
summary: The main nerve of the leg, running from the lower spinal cord down the thigh to the foot.

layers.basics: The sciatic nerve carries commands to the muscles of the leg and the signals of touch back from it. It is the large nerve of the hind limb, running down the leg from the hip region.
layers.deeper: A human also has a sciatic nerve, the longest and widest single nerve of the body, formed from spinal nerves of the lower back and sacrum and supplying the back of the thigh, the lower leg and the foot.
layers.expert: The model draws a thin cable down the leg. Its exact route and branches in a robin are not drawn from a dissection. There is no separate card for that nerve in the human body, so the human match is the general Peripheral nerves card.

facts: the muscles and skin of the leg
longest and widest nerve of the body

title: Vagus nerves
summary: The tenth cranial nerve: a long pair of nerves from the brain to the organs of the chest and gut.

layers.basics: The two vagus nerves run from the brain down the neck. They carry signals that slow the heart, and they also supply the lungs and the gut. They are not wing or leg nerves: they lead from the brain itself and not from the spinal cord.
layers.deeper: In humans the vagus supplies parasympathetic (calming, "rest and digest") nerve fibres to almost all the organs from the neck to the transverse colon from the neck to the transverse colon; its right branch slows the heart. The same general plan holds for other vertebrates, but a robin's vagus is not described in detail.
layers.expert: The model draws a thin cable on each side of the neck; the real nerve has many branches. There is no separate card for that nerve in the human body, so the human match is the general Peripheral nerves card.

facts: heart, lungs and gut (in humans; the general vertebrate plan)

title: Syrinx: where the song is made
summary: The syrinx is the bird's voice box, at the base of the windpipe where it forks, not in the throat.

layers.basics: A bird's throat (the larynx) does not make its song. The sound is made lower down, deep in the chest, in the syrinx. It sits where the windpipe splits to go to the two lungs. Soft tissue folds in each bronchus vibrate as air passes, and muscles change their tension. In some songbirds the two sides are controlled separately; that has not been shown for the robin.
layers.deeper: In songbirds the syrinx is the tracheobronchial form: the lower trachea and the upper bronchi. The tracheal rings are mostly complete; the bronchial rings are C-shaped, with smooth muscle in the open part. Experiments on other songbirds point to two soft lips, the labia, as the main vibrating parts.
layers.expert: The syrinx is drawn at true size, a few millimetres wide, and simplified. The model windpipe is about 2 mm across; real dimensions vary between birds.

facts: where the windpipe forks, above the lungs

ext.title: Goller and Larsen 1997: A new mechanism of sound generation in songbirds (PNAS 94: 14787-14791)

title: Pessulus
summary: A small bony wedge at the fork of the windpipe, between the two bronchi.

layers.basics: The pessulus stands in the middle of the fork like the point of a Y, between the two bronchi. In songbirds it is bony. Air flows on both sides of it.
layers.deeper: It is a support at the fork: in experiments on songbirds it was not found to be what vibrates. This replaces the older idea that it makes sound.
layers.expert: Goller and Larsen (1997) show the ossified pessulus in their diagram of the syrinx at rest but do not describe it as a vibrating part. The model draws a small wedge.

facts: a structural support at the fork, not a sound source

ext.title: Goller and Larsen 1997: A new mechanism of sound generation in songbirds (PNAS 94: 14787-14791)

title: Tympaniform membranes
summary: Thin membranes in the wall of each bronchus that vibrate to make the sound.

layers.basics: The tympaniform membranes are thin sheets in the walls of each bronchus. Air from the lungs flows past them. For a long time they were thought to be the part that vibrates to make the sound, like the reed of a clarinet.
layers.deeper: Experiments disproved the simple version of that idea: songbirds whose medial membranes were put out of action could still sing nearly normally. The membranes may still shape or help the sound; the soft lips (labia) in the bronchus are the likely sound source.
layers.expert: In Goller and Larsen's experiment the membrane area was replaced by a hole in four zebra finches and three cardinals; calls and song stayed nearly intact but were generally quieter, with small changes in pitch. The model draws the membranes as small discs and does not draw the labia.

facts: not the principal sound source; may help shape the sound

ext.title: Goller and Larsen 1997: A new mechanism of sound generation in songbirds (PNAS 94: 14787-14791)

title: Syringeal muscles
summary: Small muscles that tune the syrinx; songbirds control them more finely than any other birds.

layers.basics: Muscles on the outside of each bronchus change the tension of the syrinx and change the pitch. Songbirds have the finest control of these muscles of any bird, which allows their wide range of songs.
layers.deeper: The intrinsic muscles are in the syrinx; the extrinsic muscles, such as the sternotrachealis, run from outside.
layers.expert: The intrinsic muscles lie in the syrinx itself and the extrinsic muscles, such as the sternotrachealis, run to it from outside. The model draws one band on each bronchus.

title: Rings of the windpipe and bronchi
summary: The rings of cartilage that hold the windpipe open; the bronchi have C-shaped rings.

layers.basics: The trachea is stiffened by rings of cartilage, mostly complete. The bronchi have C-shaped rings with smooth muscle along the open part.
layers.deeper: The spacing changes near the syrinx.
layers.expert: The rings are stiff and keep the windpipe open while the bronchial half-rings leave a soft wall; the model draws 9 complete rings and 8 C-shaped rings on each bronchus, a drawing choice and not a count.

title: Bronchus
summary: One of the two tubes that carry air from the syrinx to the lungs.

layers.basics: The bronchi carry air from the fork of the windpipe to each lung.
layers.deeper: The syrinx covers the lowest part of the trachea and the upper bronchi.
layers.expert: Drawn leaving the fork at 40 degrees.

title: Sclera
summary: The tough white outer wall of the eyeball.

layers.basics: The sclera is the tough outer wall of the eyeball, made of collagen fibres. It supports and protects the eye and is the part that shows white in a human eye.
layers.deeper: In a bird the front of the sclera holds the ring of small bones. A bird's eye is not round but flatter, and the ring and sclera hold that shape rigid.
layers.expert: The sclera has two layers in birds. The model draws it as a shell, whose thickness is exaggerated.

title: Scleral ring: small bones in the eye
summary: A ring of small bone plates in the front of the sclera, round the cornea.

layers.basics: In the front of a bird's eye there is a ring of thin overlapping bony plates (scleral ossicles) set in the sclera. They hold the shape of the eye and give the focusing muscles something to pull on.
layers.deeper: A ring is also seen in reptiles and some other vertebrates; mammals lack it. The ossicles lie on the border between the sclera and the cornea and have mechanical roles in focusing by moving the cornea and lens.
layers.expert: Birds have 12 to 18 plates, 14 most commonly, but this was not counted on a robin. The model draws one ring.

facts: none: mammals lack a scleral ring

title: Cornea
summary: The clear front window of the eye that does most of the focusing.

layers.basics: The cornea is the clear front window of the eye. Light passes through it first, and it bends the light as it enters the eye.
layers.deeper: Some birds also have a second set of muscles that change the curve of the cornea, giving them a wider range of focus than mammals have.
layers.expert: The shell of the cornea is exaggerated in thickness in the model. Whether a robin has those muscles is not stated.

title: Iris and pupil
summary: The coloured ring that sets the size of the pupil.

layers.basics: The iris is the ring of muscle round the pupil that sets how much light enters. A robin's eye looks black, with a dark brown iris.
layers.deeper: In birds the iris muscles also help move the lens and cornea to focus. A bird's iris can be coloured in many species; the robin's is dark.
layers.expert: The model draws a flat ring.

title: Lens
summary: The lens focuses light on the retina.

layers.basics: The lens sits behind the pupil and focuses light on the retina. Muscles round it change its shape to focus on near and far.
layers.deeper: Birds have ciliary muscles that change the shape of the lens quickly and more than in mammals. These muscles attach to the lens capsule by fibres and are anchored on the ring of small bones.
layers.expert: The lens is drawn as an ellipsoid. In a bird the lens is pushed far forward, which increases the size of the image on the retina.

title: Vitreous body
summary: The clear jelly that fills the eyeball behind the lens.

layers.basics: The vitreous is the clear jelly that fills most of the eyeball behind the lens. It holds the retina in place and light passes through it.
layers.deeper: The eye is divided by the lens into a front part, filled with a watery fluid, and a back part filled with the vitreous. The pecten reaches into the vitreous.
layers.expert: The model draws a translucent sphere. The volume is not given.

title: Choroid
summary: A dark, blood-rich layer behind the retina.

layers.basics: The choroid is a dark layer between the retina and the sclera that is rich in blood vessels. The vessels feed the outer retina, and the dark pigment (melanin) cuts down reflections inside the eye.
layers.deeper: A bird's retina is largely free of its own blood vessels, so it depends on the choroid and the pecten for supply.
layers.expert: The model draws a thin dark shell. The thickness is not drawn to scale.

title: Retina
summary: The light-sensitive layer at the back of the eye; click to look inside it.

layers.basics: The retina is the screen at the back of the eye. It is made of cells that respond to light and pass signals along the optic nerve. Use the button to look inside it.
layers.deeper: A bird's retina has rods for dim light and cones for colour; most birds have four kinds of cone. It is largely free of blood vessels, which are in the choroid and the pecten instead.
layers.expert: The scene shows a photoreceptor and a cryptochrome hypothesis (see that card). Photoreceptor densities are known for other birds (house sparrow about 400,000 per square millimetre) but none is stated for a robin.

facts: rods and cones (about four cone kinds in most birds)

title: Pecten: the pleated fold in the eye
summary: The pecten is a pleated, blood-rich fold that stands out from the retina into the jelly, found only in birds.

layers.basics: In birds a pleated, blood-rich fold, the pecten, stands out from where the optic nerve enters the eye and reaches into the jelly. It is found in birds only, and its job is still debated.
layers.deeper: It has blood vessels and dark pigment cells and no muscle or nerve fibres. The pleated type has 5 to 30 pleats. Ideas for its job: feeding the retina, shading it from glare, and helping detect moving objects.
layers.expert: The Bird vision page calls the pecten "a poorly understood body". The model draws seven pleats, a choice. The question of its main job is real and open.

open_questions: What is the main job of the pecten: feeding the retina, controlling the vitreous pH, absorbing stray light, or all of them?

title: Optic nerve
summary: The cable of nerve fibres from the retina to the brain.

layers.basics: The optic nerve is the cable of nerve fibres that carries signals from the retina to the brain. It leaves the back of the eye where the pecten stands.
layers.deeper: Birds have a high number of neurons in the optic nerve. The place where it leaves the retina has no photoreceptors, the blind spot.
layers.expert: The model draws a cable. The real fibre count is not stated.

title: Inside a feather
summary: A flight feather is a tree: a shaft, side branches (barbs), twigs (barbules) and tiny hooks that zip the vane together.

layers.basics: Look closely at a feather and you find a branching structure. From the central shaft (the rachis) the side branches (barbs) grow out in a row, and from each barb grow even finer twigs, the barbules. The barbules of neighbouring barbs overlap, and tiny hooks hold them together, so the vane is a smooth sheet that holds back most of the air. If you pull it apart, the hooks re-engage when you stroke it back, which is what a bird does when it preens.
layers.deeper: The barbules on a flight feather of species from a hummingbird to a condor are spaced only 8 to 16 micrometres apart. The shaft is made of bundles of 3-nanometre keratin filaments embedded in an amorphous keratin matrix.
layers.expert: Sizes drawn in the scene: only the barbule spacing (8 to 16 µm) is a published measurement; the barb and barbule lengths and thicknesses, and the number of hooks, are illustrative.

facts: 3 nm diameter, in the shaft's cortex

ext.title: The feather's multi-functional structure across nano to macro scales inspires hierarchical design (J. R. Soc. Interface 22(225), 2025)

title: Barb
summary: A barb is one of the side branches of a feather's shaft; a row of them makes the vane.

layers.basics: Each barb is a thin rod that grows from the shaft at an angle. A feather vane has hundreds of them side by side.
layers.deeper: Along each barb, barbules branch to both sides.
layers.expert: The lengths and thicknesses drawn are illustrative.

facts: branch of the rachis, bears barbules

title: Barbule: the hooked twigs
summary: The barbules are the fine twigs of the barbs; the hooks of one barbule catch the next.

layers.basics: Each barb carries a row of barbules on each side. The barbules that face the tip of the feather have little hooks; those that face the base have a ridge where the hooks catch. The result is a zip. A barbule is a few micrometres thick and made of dead cells full of keratin. Use the button to see the molecule that links the keratin together.
layers.deeper: Neighbouring barbules sit 8 to 16 micrometres apart.
layers.expert: Each barbule is a chain of dead, keratin-filled cells; the keratin is held together by sulfur bridges.

ext.title: The feather's multi-functional structure across nano to macro scales inspires hierarchical design (J. R. Soc. Interface 22(225), 2025)

title: Hooklets (barbicels)
summary: The tiny hooks on the barbules that grip the next barbule like the loops of a zip.

layers.basics: At the end of a barbule are minute hooks, barbicels, that catch on the ridge of the next barbule. Down feathers lack them, so their barbules float free.
layers.deeper: This is what turns a loose set of branches into a continuous vane.
layers.expert: The hooklets are drawn illustratively: their size and number are not measured.

title: Pigment granules
summary: Brown and black feather colour comes from granules of melanin inside the barbs.

layers.basics: Colour in a feather is mostly made by pigment. The brown of a robin's back is melanin, in small granules inside the barbs and barbules. Use the button to see a molecule on the way to melanin.
layers.deeper: Melanin is made from the amino acid tyrosine through L-DOPA. Whether the orange of the breast is a type of melanin, phaeomelanin, or a carotenoid is not settled.
layers.expert: The granule size and number drawn are illustrative.

title: Inside the flight muscle
summary: The flight muscle is a bundle of long fibres, packed with energy-making mitochondria and fed by many fine blood vessels.

layers.basics: A muscle is made of long cells called fibres. In a flight muscle each fibre is packed with mitochondria, the parts of the cell that burn fuel with oxygen to make the energy molecule ATP. Between the fibres run fine blood vessels. Click a mitochondrion and press the button to see ATP.
layers.deeper: The fibres contract by filaments sliding past each other. The energy comes from ATP, made in the mitochondria and used by the motor protein myosin.
layers.expert: Sizes in the scene are illustrative; the numbers of fibres and mitochondria drawn are for clarity.

title: Muscle fibre
summary: A flight muscle fibre is one long cell, many times longer than it is wide.

layers.basics: Each fibre is a single long cell with many nuclei, filled with bundles of contracting filaments. It is surrounded by capillaries.
layers.deeper: Contraction comes from the sliding of thick and thin filaments.
layers.expert: The fibre drawn is a tube; real fibres are more varied in size.

title: Mitochondria
summary: Mitochondria make most of the muscle's ATP by burning fuel with oxygen.

layers.basics: Mitochondria are the powerhouses of the cell. Flight uses a lot of energy, so flight muscle is packed with them. They make the energy molecule ATP.
layers.deeper: Oxidative phosphorylation across their inner membrane makes most of the ATP.
layers.expert: Their size and number in the scene are illustrative.

title: Inside a hollow bone
summary: A hollow bone is a thin wall of dense bone round an air-filled space braced by struts.

layers.basics: A cut across a hollow bird bone shows a thin ring of hard bone round an empty (air-filled) space, crossed by thin struts like those in a bridge. The wall is made of bone cells in a framework of protein and mineral.
layers.deeper: Bone cells (osteocytes) live in tiny holes in the wall and keep it alive. The struts stiffen the tube against bending and crushing.
layers.expert: Sizes in the scene are illustrative.

title: Wall of compact bone
summary: The thin, dense wall of a hollow bone.

layers.basics: The wall is dense bone that carries most of the load. Because it is far from the centre of the tube, it makes the tube stiff for little weight.
layers.deeper: Bone is a composite of mineral and protein fibres.
layers.expert: The thickness is illustrative.

title: Strut (trabecula)
summary: Thin struts crossing the hollow of a bone, like the braces in a bridge.

layers.basics: Thin rods of bone cross the hollow space inside many bird bones. They brace the wall against bending and buckling.
layers.deeper: Their arrangement follows the loads on the bone.
layers.expert: The struts are arranged along the loads on the bone; the model draws a few straight rods across the hollow, which is a simplification of a real bone's irregular braces.

title: Bone cell (osteocyte)
summary: The living cell inside a bone, in a tiny pocket of the hard wall.

layers.basics: Osteocytes are the long-lived cells of bone. Each sits in a small space and reaches out to its neighbours with fine arms. Use the button to look inside a cell.
layers.deeper: They sense strain and direct the repair of bone.
layers.expert: An osteocyte is far smaller than the bone it lies in and sits in a small pocket (a lacuna) of the wall; the model draws the cells on the surface so they can be seen, and their size is illustrative.

title: Inside the retina
summary: The retina is a screen of light-sensing cells; a protein called cryptochrome is one candidate for a magnetic sensor.

layers.basics: Light entering the eye falls on the retina, which is made of layers of cells. The light-sensing cells, the photoreceptors, hold the molecule retinal, which changes shape when it catches a photon. Some of the retina's proteins, the cryptochromes, may help the robin sense Earth's magnetic field; that is an unproven idea.
layers.deeper: The photoreceptors send signals through other retinal neurons to the optic nerve. A bird's retina is largely free of blood vessels; it is fed from the choroid and the pecten.
layers.expert: The scene is a schematic: the cell shapes and sizes are illustrative, and the place of cryptochrome in a particular cell type is not drawn as a measurement.

title: Photoreceptor cell
summary: A photoreceptor catches light with the molecule retinal and turns it into a nerve signal.

layers.basics: Photoreceptors are the retina's light-sensing cells. Their outer part is full of membranes carrying a light-sensitive protein with retinal. A photon changes retinal's shape and starts a chain of events that ends in a nerve signal. Use the button to see retinal.
layers.deeper: Birds have rods for dim light and cones, with several kinds for colour.
layers.expert: Sizes drawn are illustrative.

title: Cryptochrome 4 (a hypothesis for the magnetic sensor)
summary: A light-sensitive protein that carries the molecule FAD; it is a candidate for the robin's magnetic sensor.

layers.basics: Cryptochrome is a protein that holds a flavin molecule (FAD). When light excites the FAD, an electron jumps along a chain of tryptophan units in the protein, leaving a pair of molecules with unpaired electrons. Earth's magnetic field could affect how long such a pair lasts. This is a hypothesis for how a robin senses the field, not a proved mechanism. Use the button to see FAD.
layers.deeper: In the laboratory, robin cryptochrome 4 shows a four-step electron transfer along tryptophan units and a radical pair lasting about 100 nanoseconds, and it is more magnetically sensitive than chicken or pigeon cryptochrome 4. The effects were measured at about 30 millitesla, not at Earth-strength field. Whether it works as the compass in the bird is not shown.
layers.expert: See the compass card for the behavioural evidence and what is missing: the radical pair is about ten times too short-lived for Earth-strength sensitivity unless the protein is anchored and linked to signalling partners.

facts: hypothesis (in vitro evidence at about 30 mT)
open_questions: Is cryptochrome 4 the magnetic sensor in the living robin eye?

title: Bird
summary: A bird is a feathered animal descended from theropod dinosaurs; the park's bird is a European robin, standing on the boulder.

layers.basics: Birds are the living descendants of feathered dinosaurs. Most fly, with wings, hollow bones, a keeled breastbone and a lung that works with air sacs; some, such as ostriches, do not. The bird in this park is a European robin, standing on the boulder. Click it for its card, or use "Show where it is" to fly to it.
layers.deeper: Birds are theropod dinosaurs, warm-blooded, with feathers, a four-chambered heart and a lung in which air flows in one direction. Zoom in on the robin to see all of that, down to the molecules of its feathers and muscles.
layers.expert: The old cartoon birds are gone; the robin is a data model built at the size of a typical adult. The park is a simplified scene, not a scan of a real place.

facts: a European robin, about 14 cm long
